utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We'll continue to -- with the cross-examination, but, Mr. Lukic, later today we'll deal with a few procedural matters, and the Chamber would very much appreciate if you could give an update about Plan A or Plan B, starting on the 10th of August. Meanwhile, Mr. Kelecevic, I'd like to remind you that you're bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Registrar, I finally would like to check whether the videolink is functioning well. Can you hear me, can you see us?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honour, we can see and hear you clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the same is true in the other direction. Mr. Lukic will now continue his cross-examination -- his re-examination, yes, of course. I misspoke, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General. Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will start with something we touched upon yesterday. I'm afraid I'll eventually run out of time so I'd rather deal with this now. At page 37292 of yesterday's transcript concerning P7479 -- well, I'll read out the question and your answer and then I'll have a question for you. Lines 15 through 18, [In English] I'll quote: "Now this is a reflection that by early April 1992 the 122nd Brigade had been deployed back to Bosnia from Croatia and was responsible for, among other places, the area of Kotor Varos; right? "A. Yes."

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please tell us what Peulic was responsible for, that is to say, the 122nd Brigade in the area of Kotor Varos. Were they responsible for the towns, villages, or something else?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'd just ask for a date reference in the question so that it's clear whether he's referring to -- or at what point Mr. Lukic is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think it was in the question: Early April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It was in my question. I hadn't been clear if it was in his. But with that clarification, I'm happy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question focuses on the responsibility of Mr. Peulic, early April 1992, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please tell us what Peulic was responsible for in the area of Kotor Varos, both in early April 1992 and later on. If you know.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade commanded by Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic was deployed at the Vlasic plateau on Mount Vlasic. The altitude there is quite high. His front line or his area of responsibility, I don't know exactly, but it followed a 20- to 25-kilometre line. That was the AOR of his brigade, including the biggest settlement in the area, Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the army was deployed into towns themselves?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only some patrols or security could be present in the town. Most of the other soldiers were at the front line because enemy forces were expected to arrive from the area of Travnik and from the direction of the Muslim-Croat forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 65 ter number 2596 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document has already been admitted into evidence as P7480. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The B/C/S version is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will -- [Interpretation] Let us look at this extract from the minutes of the 100th Session of the War Presidency on 16 October 1992 in Kotor Varos. We will require the second page in the English. The second paragraph in the English, being the last paragraph in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It reads as follows: "Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic took the floor again and pointed out that the general position and achieved agreements on population resettlement and hand-over of weapons must not be abandoned."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go one page back in the English to the first page. The last paragraph in the English version, which is the fifth paragraph in the B/C/S on page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It reads as follows: "President Nedeljko D pointed out that an International Red Cross team had been in the area again yesterday, that the negotiators had gone to Vecici too, and that the initial results from Vecici were not favourable, that they had met with the other side's representatives (Baltina), that a list containing the names of 1200 to 1500 people had been compiled, that this will require about 30 buses. Intensified activity relating to moving out should be expected in the course of the day and hand-over of weapons, and that representatives of the Red Cross and possibly journalists are expected."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, just one question. The word in brackets is it in B/C/S Baltina as translated or Bastina?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's hard to see. Could be both, but could be Bastina too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness could clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't think he can see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] The witness is able to read this, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'll ask if he knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, General, in this fifth paragraph, if you can see the parentheses, does it read Baltina or Bastina?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that area, but my guess would be that the location is on the Muslim side, if I follow the logic of the sentence. I think it is Baltina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know anything about the negotiations that took place in Vecici?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you anything specific about the negotiations. I do know that the gist of it is reflected in what Colonel Peulic said. He said that we should be persistent in collecting the weapons. He was addressing the Crisis Staff in Kotor Varos, insisting that the weapons be handed over and that the forces in Kotor Varos be disarmed. He said that the activity should continue because it was not completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of whether the arms were handed over, indeed, and whether the civilians left Vecici?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge. I don't remember that because, at that time, as I said, I was in a completely different area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I'd like to ask you about your answer provided on page 37317, line 20 till the end of the page, and it continues on to page 37318, lines 1 through 4. You were asked to answer a very complex question, and I will try to break up the question put by Mr. Traldi. To the best of your recollection, did the VRS and the 1st Krajina Corps implement the first strategic goal, i.e., separation from Muslims and Croats, by detaining and killing Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. One cannot formulate it that way. We cannot say that the VRS was doing it strategically. It wasn't engaged in any separation. The goal was always to keep those who were loyal and who forwarded the policies of Republika Srpska and who were prepared to stay in the area, to keep them in the area and include them in the armed force, rather than separating the peoples in a very determined way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next question. Did the VRS and the 1st Krajina Corps implement the first strategic goal of separation from Muslims and Croats by removing Muslims and Croats through exchanges?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One also cannot say that was the case. Those who wished to leave were allowed to go freely and safely. In such cases, the authorities and the army enabled their passage unhindered through certain areas and exchanges to take place. In my view, no pressure was made for exchanges to occur, unless there was a will on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you seek a clarification of that last answer which is a bit ambiguous, especially the "unless there was a will on both sides."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, you've heard the Judge, you've heard Judge Orie.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard him. I mean the Serb and the Muslim side agree that the exchanges be carried out. That is the core of the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I understand your answer to be: No pressure was made for exchanges to occur and that the exchanges were made only if there was a will on both sides. Is that what you meant to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, pressures don't have to come from both sides. The most important thing is here is the following: If those who wanted to leave the areas where they were, it was only natural that they would be allowed to leave, if that was their will, if that was their intention, but they were supposed to be able leave securely, safely. That is what was supposed to be ensured for them. I'm sorry, the other side. I do apologise. May I just finish explaining the sense of all of this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other side should ensure their free passage through the zone of the brigade so that they could go to the area where they said they wanted to go. So unhindered safe passage through the area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I then put one follow-up question to you. You said what was done for those who wished to leave. Were there any who'd rather stay and did not wish to leave? And what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my view, in relation to, I mean, the policy of the Serb authorities and thereby the army as well, those who wished to stay would stay and - how should I put this? - they were loyal to the authority, specifically, in this case, the authorities of Kotor Varos. They could freely live there, unhindered, take care of their own business, depending on the combat situation, whether there was firing or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have one other follow-up question. If they wished to stay but if they disagreed with the authority, at the same time not taking up weapons, what would happen to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in my view -- I mean, I'm not speaking specifically about this particular case but I'm speaking in general terms. I mean, I'm speaking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like you to talk about this specific case. And I think we're still talking about Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I cannot speak specifically about that case because, as for Kotor Varos, I wasn't there then and I did not have any detailed conversations with my officers who came to see me at the corridor to inform me about certain matters. So specifically what happened to those people who were not carrying out tasks issued by the authorities of Kotor Varos, I don't know how the civilian authorities treated them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered my question. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, my next question. The Army of Republika Srpska and the 1st Corps, were they carrying out the first strategic goal, separation from the Muslims by moving the population out?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is a categorical no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My last question, with regard to this topic, that is: The Army of Republika Srpska, the 1st Krajina Corps, were they carrying out the second strategic goal, opening the corridor by carrying out Operation Corridor?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand the essence of your question. Why the corridor was being opened? I can explain why it was being opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it in accordance with the second-mentioned strategic goal, to the extent to which you remember it, and it is the opening of the corridor and linking up with the East Bosnian Corps and Semberija.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The East Bosnian Corps and the western part of the Army of Republika Srpska -- I mean, the Eastern Bosnian Corps of the Army of Republika Srpska and the western part -- I mean, Kordun, Banija, Lika, Dalmatia, these areas where Serbs lived, that was justified and that is why it was being opened. That was the basic task for opening the corridor, that was it precisely, so that they could come unhindered from the eastern area so that they could get there. At that time even medicine could not arrive, I've already mentioned that, also oxygen bottles. And 12 babies died because of that situation in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The date before yesterday there was some discussion about Odzak. What were the forces that were in Odzak before the VRS entered Odzak?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Odzak, it was majority Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Around --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what was observed. That was the intelligence that was there, that in the broader area there were also parts of infiltrated forces from the Republic of Croatia, from the other side of the Sava river.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In Odzak and around Odzak, was there fighting before the forces of the Army of Republika Srpska entered?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was fighting. Most of it around Brod because that is where a group was infiltrated from the Croat side. And there was this family, Zecevic, and I cannot remember the name of the other ones. Quite simply, they were massacred, they were slaughtered, and the situation was very, very difficult. It was harrowing, the situation around Brod.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when that happened?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that the massacre took place on the 26th of March, the 26th of March. And later on, in succession, this went on until May and mid-June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just for clarity, which year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. P2886, please. Could we have a look at that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a fairly long document: Analysis of activity concerning elements of combat readiness in 1992. My colleague Mr. Traldi showed you page 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I would kindly ask to have page 12 in the English version and page 17 in the B/C/S version. In the English version, it's the last paragraph. And in the B/C/S version, the second paragraph from the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is a reference to the number of persons taken prisoner, and it says that there is a certain number of prisoners of war, over 9.200 prisoners were exchanged, and you were asked about this. Let me ask you the following. A combatant in the field that finds a military-aged man in the field, does he have the right to assess whether that person is a combatant or not?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He does have that right, if he can assess that or establish that. If not, such a person is brought in so that other organs can assess whether that person is a combatant or a civilian. Whether that person is a member of an army, that would be a better term. It is more specific to say a member of an army rather than just combatant, which is a more general term.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On transcript page 37221, from line 23 to 25, in response to a question along these lines, there is the answer you gave and I'm going to quote it: [In English] "Well, again, I'm telling you, I have no way of knowing whether it was a civilian or a military conscript until certain checks were completed." [Interpretation] What kind of checks, General? Who carries out these checks?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who carries out checks as to whether somebody is a civilian or a combatant?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We could not hear the witness. Now Mr. Lukic is speaking at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. The Judge is saying something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreters noted, Mr. Lukic, that you interrupted when the witness was still speaking --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and, therefore, they couldn't hear him. Could you please resume --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I'll see where we -- [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So your answer has not been recorded. After reading this out, I asked you what kind of checks are carried out. Who carries out these checks, whether somebody is a soldier or a civilian, if that person is brought in.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it all depends on the place where that person was taken prisoner, if I can put it that way, or where that person is captured. If it is in the area of combat activity, if it was on the front line itself, a soldier cannot carry out such a check at the front line. The only thing that can he do is take that person through the combat order, hand that person over to the civilian authorities, and let them establish who this person is. The army doesn't have time to do that and it is not fully equipped to carry out such checks then. Those basic checks, as in taking person's details, that can be carried out by some orders behind the lines. But at the front line itself there is no time for that kind of thing and such checks cannot be carried out there. That has to be done either by civilians or the organs of the military police, if that unit does have a police. Not each and every unit has its own military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If such a person was brought to Manjaca, who carries out the checks then, and what kind of checks?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that person was brought to Manjaca and there is a procedure at the gate itself, at the entrance itself, because Manjaca is a fenced-off area, it's a big area, it used to be a military facility. How do I put this? There was this manufacturing there and so on and so forth. So at the gate itself, a check is carried out as to who it is that's coming in. Then the person is being taken to a particular facility and handed over to the security organs that carry out this check once the person is already within the facility. And then lists are created, name, surname, date of birth, all these details that are required so that these persons could be on various lists. So every person that entered Manjaca had to be recorded in these lists. And I'm convinced that the police, the military police, did that at Manjaca. As far as Manjaca is concerned, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one follow-up question there. Are you aware of persons being checked at the gate, that it was established that those persons were civilians and therefore they were not further admitted into the camp but, rather, sent home because the first check showed that they were civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know of such a check, that a soldier could take him back immediately and say, You cannot go in. I know of one case only and I mentioned it yesterday. The civilian authorities tried -- there were about ten or eight dead bodies. They tried to hand them over and that was not accepted so they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness -- Witness, I'm not talking about dead bodies. I'm talking about living persons arriving at the gate and at the first check that it was established, or perhaps immediately after that, that they were not members of the army. Are you aware of any such persons then being released and being sent back home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not aware of any such check or any such person. And if that did happen, then the person at the gate did not act properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer is not entirely clear to me. I have one other question going back to the text which is before you about the exchanges. I slowly read what it says. It says: "We achieved significant results in activities related to prisoner-of-war exchanges." And then it further explains that 9.200 prisoners were exchanged, of which 2.300 were military personnel. Now this suggests that the other close to 7.000 were not military personnel but they're still described as prisoners of war and prisoners having been exchanged. Do you have any comment on the -- what the text suggests, that it is 7.000 who are not military men nevertheless being exchanged, as the document says, as prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This refers to the entire year and the area of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps, about 9.200. You know how big the area was. I don't want to repeat that. 2.300 military men. I cannot give any comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean, how this went -- I mean, I cannot give any comment, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, the Judge asked you about the 7.000. How did their exchange occur so that they were exchanged as POWs where it had been established they were -- that they were not military personnel. So you were asked about the 7.000 by the Judge. Do you have an explanation?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an exchange with the opposing side. On the opposing side, there were also many people of Serb ethnicity who were taken prisoner by the other side. Those exchange commissions were in contact and the exchange took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's look at P230 next.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just for the record, this is Exhibit P230. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were asked about this document yesterday. At the beginning of it, it is stated that on the 13th of July, 1992, a visit was made possible to Manjaca camp and that all of the requests made by the seven-member delegation were agreed to. They spent three days in the camp, prisoners were allowed to write to their families. They were allowed to register the prisoners and to talk to them alone "without our presence." They also inspected their medical care and diet. Yesterday at transcript page 37228, lines 5 through 15, Mr. Traldi suggested that Colonel Vukelic reported that the Red Cross team interrupted the visit and any further talks because they were not allowed to meet the four prisoners designated by Colonel Vukelic as criminals. They also objected to the amount of food given to the prisoners and their loss of weight, as well as to the traces of blood visible on the prisoners. And I wanted to read out a portion of this document and see what it says: "The entire team broke off today's discussion and visits [sic] to the camp because, allegedly, they had not been allowed to meet with four prisoners (criminals) on whom a military court had earlier been passed judgement. The representatives were shown their sentences and were even allowed to talk to them freely. They were surprised by this, and they made observations about the quantities of food, loss of weight of the prisoners, the risk of an epidemic breaking out and the like. They had no valid points to corroborate their observations, and the suggestion to have a group of medical experts examine them was rejected. Specifically they demanded the release of 19 prisoners on account of their state of health. As a matter of fact, these individuals were among the greatest extremists. They rejected our explanation that these people were guaranteed improved medical care, and that they could see it for themselves. They levelled accusations at the treatment of the prisoners and they claimed to have seen fresh traces of blood and had no answer to the question of the prison commander as to" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we have the second page in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have the second page in English. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "... why they had not allowed a doctor (one of the prisoners) to establish that immediately." General, do you remember this report and do you know what followed in further discussions with the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this report specifically. How could I? In any case, I remember some of the procedures. I can say the following. Those who were included in discussions concerning food, I claim responsibly that they enjoyed the same food as the fighters at the front lines. I could observe that when I visited a hangar, a hall, accommodating those prisoners. I talked to them in person, and none of them complained about that. I always conduct such conversations in a humane way, without any tension or threat. It was a civilised conversation I had with them, and they didn't say anything of the sort. I couldn't, of course, visit all of the hangars and visit some three and a half thousand of them, but I think I saw some 6- to 700 people. As for their receiving small quantities of food, I can't believe that. First of all, the military camp warden enjoyed my greatest respect, who was a very orderly, diligent officer who kept things well in order. Second of all, these prisoners, or inmates, whatever we call them, never left Manjaca to work on fortifying certain positions which was the case with the Serbs in other theatres of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. As for the medical care and the assertion that the 19 were not receiving medical care, I remember very well that, according to the list, 92 people from Manjaca who were singled out by the medical commission were sent to Geneva for treatment. I can't remember any longer what else you wanted me to say. As for the traces of blood, this is the first time I hear about that and that no possibility was given to investigate that and how that blood came to be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The situation described in the document is July. You said you went to Manjaca in late August 1992. What do you know specifically about the situation mid-July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I didn't say that I visited it in late August. I can't say precisely what the date was when I visited it. If I said so, even now I can't claim or say what the date was. I visited one of the halls and I don't know when exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement I read: "On one occasion, approximately in late August 1992, I personally visited the Manjaca centre." You have attested to the truth of that. Is your evidence to be understood now that you don't know whether it was late August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It was precisely that way. If it has to do with the military prisoners who were transferred from Omarska and Keraterm because they were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness -- Witness, I'm only asking about the date, nothing else at this moment, and I asked you where in your statement you say it was late August that you went there, that you now say you don't know when it was. Is that your testimony now, that you don't remember that it was in late August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember that it was -- now why am I making this link in terms of dates? Because the prisoners in Omarska arrived between the 6th and 10th of August. Therefore, they could not have been there in July. There were some prisoners there who had been there previously. I was talking about those who arrived from the general area of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the document before us is the 16th of July, so that was what the questions were about, and that was Manjaca camp. If you say no opportunity was given to further investigate the traces of blood, then that was in -- established in July; at least it was seen at that point in time. Do you know any further specifics about what happened in July in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd rather not comment on July. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only know about those I talked to in August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so it was in August. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, what is your knowledge about the release of people from Manjaca? Do you have any personal knowledge or did you participate personally?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did you have in mind the exchange of those prisoners or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood your question. President Karadzic, sometime in early December, although I don't know the exact date, sent an order requesting that the POWs from Manjaca be exchanged and the camp disbanded. It was supposed to be done safely and securely. The exchange was supposed to take place via Banja Luka-Laktasi-Topola-Gradiska and across the Sava into Croatia. The exchange took place in some three to four days because not all of them left at once. They left in groups of some 20 buses so around 1.000 people could be exchanged in one go. The exchange continued. I'm personally familiar with a case in the village of Klasnice near Laktasi. We had information that an ambush was set up there in order to make the passage of prisoners and buses impossible and to have them killed or something else. I'm not sure. General Talic personally issued an order to me, because I was well familiar with that area, to go there and check the situation. When I arrived, the situation was quite heated and difficult. Some people were there who simply wanted to block the passage of the column. With the assistance of an officer, I explained to the group what the consequences could be. I told them that the order had come from the Supreme Commander and that it had to go through. I won't elaborate much further, but --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can't hear the witness because of the quality of sound.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried to deal with it in a safe way and I talked to those people trying to prevent it from happening. Had something of the sort indeed taken place, it would have been fatal, not only for the city of Banja Luka but for the VRS as well. Because I know what a POW is, I know that such a person needs to be made and kept safe and ensured passage. Later on, the military police also secured certain check-points, making sure that the column passed through safely in the three or four occasions that the exchange took place. Some 3- to 3.500 POWs were exchanged without any incidents. Perhaps a bus window was broken here and there but that was all. I know that it was done in terms of exchanging those people who were at Manjaca. With that, the camp at Manjaca was practically shut down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at P2243 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Under seal, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under seal. Mr. Lukic, I'm looking at the clock. If you go to a new subject, perhaps it would be better to take the break first.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can go to -- have a break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We have a break of 20 minutes. We'd like to see you back after the break, Witness. Mr. Lukic, are you on track as far as time is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Today it goes a bit slower. I agreed with my colleague Mr. Traldi and I will take next half an hour and leave him half an hour in the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see Mr. Traldi is nodding yes, so apparently he agrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take the break and resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I was told -- P2243, under seal. I have been informed, General, that you don't have this, so we are going to see it on our screens. I'm going to read out something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Again, the document's under seal and for reasons I'd ask that we move into private session or at least not broadcast it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I said under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Lukic said under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And what I'd intended that should indicate at least that it not -- an instruction that it not be broadcast which hadn't yet been given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree. But I take it that Mr. Registrar is already drawing that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, we have to move into private session if any part of it is read.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, you were asked if Zeljaja was removed. Let me ask you this: Were you ever informed that Zeljaja killed women or children?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never informed of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Without referring to a source, but were you familiar with these documents during the war?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't familiar with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we next have P2900, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is a document from the CSB commission entitled: "Work of investigation centres in the region - documents." Therefore, it is a police report. I'd like direct your attention to page 3 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could we go back to page 2 first.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you can see on the screen, the report was compiled by the Security Services Centre in Banja Luka. The title of the report is: Concerning the situation as found and questions relating to prisoners, collection centres, resettlement, and the role of the SJB in connection with these activities. The first municipality in line is Prijedor and its reception centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we need to go to the next page in both versions, which is page 3. In English ... [In English] Can we see the top of the page, please. We have to go one page back in English version, I'm sorry. There is obviously missing one part in English version. I will read it. This the first paragraph on this page in B/C/S version. We will ask for this translation to be revised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I quote: "In order to solve the problem that had arisen, the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Prijedor decided to organise reception and accommodation in the settlement of Trnopolje for persons who sought protection and that prisoners of war should be held for processing in the building of the Keraterm RO in Prijedor or in the administrative building and work-shop of the RZR in Omarska."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I was going to say, I think, the same thing as you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's: "In order to solve the problem that had arisen, the Crisis Staff," it's in the middle of the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm ... I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, did the Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality inform the 1st Krajina Corps about this; if you know?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of the 1st Corps being informed. I do know about the camp in Trnopolje. In my understanding, it was open-type centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need page 4 in the English in the same document, the first paragraph, and page 4 in the B/C/S, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please follow the last paragraph which reads: "On 27 May 1992, pursuant to the decision of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Prijedor, all the prisoners from the Keraterm facility in Prijedor were transferred to the facility in Omarska. Under the same decision, the Omarska facility was placed under the direct supervision of the police and the army. The police, i.e., Omarska police station, was charged with the immediate security of the administration building itself, the workshops and the garages for the work machinery, while the army took over in-depth security in the form of sentry posts and the mining of certain areas as they saw fit." Can you tell us what "in-depth security" is; and do you know at what distance the army was from the facility where the prisoners were kept?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not personally visit the camp at Trnopolje, and I'm not familiar with the location. I do know that in-depth security is always away from the facility along certain axes from which potential attacks or interventions on the facility can be expected, including attacks on the people accommodated there, regardless of the side included in such incidents. If the army participated, and judging by the document it did, according to the Crisis Staff, it was duty-bound to secure the facility so that only checked personnel could enter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just to put on the record I see the witness has been making some notes, and I'd just ask if he'd have an objection to a copy being made and sent to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Mr. Traldi observed that you're making notes. Is it -- do you want to share that with the Prosecution so that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm just noting down a date or two. If need be, I can tear it up now, this second, before your eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The question was not whether you wanted to tear it but the question was whether you wanted to share it. And by destroying it, I take it that the answer is no, this is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would write down a date or two so as to remind myself where I was at the time. That's the gist of it. If I had been warned not to keep notes, I would not have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, the witness apparently is not inclined to share it with you. There's only an invitation. I leave it to that. Unless you come up with something else. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In the same document, we need page 6 in the English and page 8 in the B/C/S. In the English, we're interested in the third paragraph under the heading of: The role of Prijedor SJB and its personnel. In the B/C/S, it is the last paragraph on that page, also the third from the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It reads: "Pursuant to the decision of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Prijedor, police personnel attended to the physical security of the Keraterm facility in Prijedor, and subsequently the transportation of the prisoners to the RZR ... in Omarska and the physical security of this facility as well. On the basis of the results of operative processing of prisoners, the police found the persons who were wanted and brought them to Omarska. After questioning, the police also looked after security during transportation to the Manjaca army camp or to the Open Reception Centre in Trnopolje." General, do you know whether the 1st Krajina Corps ever drafted reports on the work of Omarska, Keraterm, or Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. Sometimes the Crisis Staff provided reports, but I don't remember this particular instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at 65 ter number 11 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, before we do that, could we turn -- could we go back to page 3 in the English of this document. Witness, I read the following part of -- and I must admit that I don't know where it is in the B/C/S version, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What do you want to read if I may help?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's the paragraph that starts with --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I cannot ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "... the facilities of the Keraterm work organisation," that's the paragraph I wanted to read from.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, as a matter of fact, let me just see what ... no, it's the -- yes, but I still have to find it in English. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- 4, first paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know yet which ... I made a mistake. It may be the second paragraph. I read the following in what seems to be the second paragraph in your language. It reads: "The SJB was given the task of securing the facility with employees of the active and reserve forces of the police. Banja Luka CSB and the Banja Luka Corps Command were informed about the capture of persons and were actively involved in the solution of the situation. Mixed operations teams were set up, composed of representatives of national, public, and military security services, whose task it was to carry out operative processing of all the prisoners and to determine the degree of their personal responsibility in the armed conflict." Could you tell us anything about these mixed operations where military security was involved to carry out the operative processing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, specifically as for the processing of these persons who came to these reception camps, I don't know, except for Colonel Majstorovic, that any of the members of the army were among these persons who were in charge of these operative checks. These operative checks, in my view, involved, first and foremost, the activities of these persons, whether -- whether they had taken part in fighting, whether they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'm not primarily interested to hear what exactly the checks were about. Do you know where these combined teams, including military secret services, were doing this check?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, Colonel Majstorovic was in that camp, Omarska, just in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because in your earlier answers it transpired, more or less, that the army had nothing to do what happened in the camp; whereas I now understand that -- from this document that mixed operation teams were working in those camps, including military security services. Is that something you can confirm or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Later on, I found out - later on - that Colonel Majstorovic was involved in these checks. I don't know whether someone from the military organisation that -- decided he should be there or whether this was done specifically by the town of Prijedor or, rather, the police, the SUP of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But "mixed operations teams" suggests that military and civilian or police authorities were working together in a team formation. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can just present some assumptions. I personally do not know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we're not interested in assumptions. If you know anything, tell us; if you don't know, tell us that you don't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have just one more document. It's 65 ter 11336.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Mr. Lukic, we don't have the document, the document with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. I will read then. We need the second page in B/C/S, and we are on the correct page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, this is a dispatch from the SJB Prijedor, that is to say, the public security station of Prijedor, that is to say, the police. What is written here is as follows. This was sent to the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Army of the Serbian Republic of BH, and the Banja Luka CSB. I quote: "We hereby inform you that, at a meeting held on the 24th of July, 1992, the War Presidency of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly adopted a decision ... pursuant to which the reserve police force presently employed should be greatly reduced and that the security for the Keraterm, Trnopolje, and Omarska Reception Centres be provided by the army. The deadline for the implementation of this decision was fixed for the 31st of July, 1992. "The army refused to assume security duties at the centres, for which our station supplies a staff of 300 police officers every day. "Therefore, we hereby inform you that we are not in a position to implement the above-mentioned decision on the reduction of the reserve police force as long as the army does not resume its duties in accordance with arrangements and decisions previously made." "Signed by the chief the security station, Simo Drljaca." General, General Kelecevic, what do you know about this? Well, if you do know anything. When did the army take over these activities? Did it play any role in these activities after the 1st of August, 1992, when Simo Drljaca wrote this dispatch?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is the following. Well, I'm saying this in terms of the importance of the content, not the specific document, because I see the time here, the 24th of July. That is when the break through the corridor is starting. Now I, as Chief of Staff, for me, to find out about this, there is no way I can find out because my activity was exclusively focused on a very, very important operation in that period. But later, I was in a position to find out from the reports of officers. So I personally do not know about this, but I know this much: That after the order of President Karadzic, the army did their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is it that you are referring to now when you say "after the order of President Karadzic, the army did their job"? What is the time-frame and what was the job?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The month of August. Was it the 10th or something like that? As far as I remember, August. And then these prisoners who, I mean, in some way -- I mean, well, they were examined and all of that, and some were supposed to be transferred to the area of the Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I take it, given the witness's comment that he doesn't know anything about it, that it's being tender from the bar table; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or at least through this witness, although the witness cannot say anything, but it's related to his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think that's how the Chamber has generally articulated the text for bar tabling documents through a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but it has been criticised many, many times by the Defence and I adjusted my language now and then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I -- but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you confirm that it's tendered in relation to the witness's evidence, not because the witness could tell us anything specific about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: On the understanding that the Defence is relying on that same approach, we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I must admit - and this is just an observation - that I'm a bit confused because the document is about security services in Keraterm, Trnopolje and Omarska; whereas the answer of the witness dealt not with security aspects of those camps but rather with what he learned later on how and when and why prisoners were transferred to other camps. I leave it to that. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document shall be assigned Exhibit Number D1111. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. We have thus completed the redirect of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General Kelecevic, thank you for having answered our questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Traldi, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Before I start, I am going to request what's left of the witness's notes, and I'd just inquire with the Registry whether there's a technical way for it to be, for instance, scanned and sent to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the first question was whether the witness was willing to share it with you. Witness, although torn apart, from what we can see here, it's still on the desk. Do you have any problems in sharing what you wrote down with the Prosecution? You're pointing at them. Is that you have no problems in sharing it? In which case, the Registrar at the far end of the videolink will take custody of your notes. But I would first like to know whether you have any problems in sharing it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no problem whatsoever. If you have a person of confidence here, then that person can come and take this straight away, and I don't mind at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, our person of confidence is the Registrar at the far end of the videolink. Could you take custody of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then, let the gentleman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the Registrar at the far end side of the videolink take custody of the notes which were torn apart by the witness and bring them to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honour, that'll be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, is it that you wanted immediately to have that scan or --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you wish the Chamber to scan the document immediately?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If it's possible in the field office, then I'd request that, just so I can determine quickly and resolve whether it's necessary to have any questions asked of the witness about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It may take until after the break before have you it, but Mr. Registrar informs me that they'll do their utmost best to have it scanned. Of course, first, I see Mr. Registrar at the far end is already recomposing the original order of the torn-apart pieces.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, it will take me a bit to put this together, but I can have it scanned and e-mail it to Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and we'll see then -- and then not only to Mr. Traldi but then also to Mr. Lukic, of course. The Registry is --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] And may I just add Your Honours, the witness made notes from yesterday and the day before but he does not have it with him so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's leave it to the notes of today and let's see what we can achieve if Mr. Traldi is that much interested to look at them. Mr. Traldi, any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Traldi:

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, I want to pick up where you left off a moment ago. During cross-examination, you testified that you did not know whether Colonel Majstorovic was at Omarska, and that's at transcript page 37265 on Tuesday. Today at temporary transcript page 30, you testified that: "As far as I know, Colonel Majstorovic was in that camp, Omarska." Did you learn this in the last two days?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I found out from Glas or some other Banja Luka newspaper about the Crisis Staff, et cetera, and that Colonel Majstorovic was on that Crisis Staff, and that surprised me quite a bit at the time. And the question in my mind was who appointed him to be there on the Crisis Staff when I know the position of the commander that the command does not accept that military personnel should be on these Crisis Staffs. So I found out that he was a member of the Crisis Staff of Prijedor from - now was it Glas or Nezavisne Novine, I cannot tell you exactly which newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, you just testified now, first, first, you testified that Colonel Majstorovic was on the Crisis Staff, I'm going to return to that point in a moment. But, first, my question had been: When did you learn that he was at Omarska, and I'll add, participating in overseeing the teams of interrogators? When did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I learned that maybe after the war. Let's be clear on this. At that time I did not find out that Majstorovic was a member of the Crisis Staff either.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And, sir, your testimony on Tuesday that did you not know on Tuesday when I asked you the question whether he was at Omarska, that was false testimony; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that he was at the Omarska facility. And I never claimed any such thing. I don't know whether he was there. I was not checking on them where they were because that's not for me to do. That is specifically up to Stevo Bogojevic, Colonel Bogojevic, his superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll leave that point aside. The other portion of your answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, Mr. Traldi. Witness, I'd like to read to you part of your testimony today. I asked you about combined teams, including military security services, where they were doing these checks. You said: "As far as I know, Colonel Majstorovic was in that camp, Omarska, just in Omarska." That's why Mr. Traldi did put to you that you gave evidence today which is not the same as you gave two days ago. Any comment where you again say now that you didn't know that he was in Omarska whereas earlier today you told, as far as you know, "he was in that camp, Omarska, just in Omarska."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the question is about this combined, or whatever you call it, Crisis Staff, I just knew about Majstorovic, that he was on that staff. And I'm saying that with full responsibility. I'm telling you how it was that I found out. It's not from military reports or that somebody asked for my approval that he should be there -- oh, all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness -- Witness, do you have an explanation as to why you said earlier today that he was in Omarska, just in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say. I mean, my assessment is -- well, it was said that most of these people, I mean, from Keraterm or, rather, from -- I mean, yeah, Keraterm were transferred to Omarska and -- I don't know. Somebody said that some witness said earlier that Colonel Majstorovic investigated or, rather, interrogated him and that he insisted -- well, I know Majstorovic personally, and then I assumed that he was in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When that question was put to you, you said he was not in Omarska. Today, not solicited in any way specifically about the whereabouts of Colonel Majstorovic, you spontaneously told us that he was in that camp, Omarska, just Omarska. I have not heard any comment on what I asked you, neither an explanation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As to the second part of that answer, sir, you claimed, even though you had not been asked about Crisis Staffs, that --

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, don't interrupt Mr. Traldi when he puts a question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, you claimed, even though you had not been asked about Crisis Staffs, that the corps command did not accept that military officers be on Crisis Staffs. As you testified earlier this week, General Talic was a member of the ARK Crisis Staff. Your evidence about this is not the truth either, is it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would rather not discuss my commander and whether he had the right to do something or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, was he on the ARK Crisis Staff, General Talic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, he was a member of the Crisis Staff. He only went there when they had things to discuss about the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered my question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Next, sir, I want to turn to your evidence about command posts. When you went to the 1KK command post in the corridor, one of the officers who remained in Banja Luka was Colonel Milutin Vukelic; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was from the political and legal sector. I don't know if he stayed in Banja Luka or went to some other units. That's something I can't say. One cannot say that he was only in Banja Luka. He was inside the area of responsibility of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 32716, page 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, this is a portion of the OTP interview of Colonel Vukelic. He's asked towards the top of the page and I'll read it slowly because it's only in English: "Okay, Colonel. And how many times did General Talic visit the Manjaca camp?" He answers: "I don't know. But the command post for the corps was there for a while." He's asked: "The command post for the 1st Krajina Corps was stationed at Manjaca camp?" And he answers: "Not at the camp. The camp were renovated stables for animals. Those were renovated for the prison. And there was a command post for a unit there, which was then used for the command of the 1st Krajina Corps." And he's asked: "And did you see General Talic at this command post at Manjaca?" And he answers: "Of course, I saw him there." Now, you testified that the 1st Krajina Corps command post was not fully operational on re-examination. The truth is the 1st Krajina Corps command post at Manjaca operated, and General Talic visited it; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm very cautious now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. "Objection" is not sufficient. You should say what the objection is based, without giving evidence yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can the General remove his headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Headphones. Could you please take off your headphones. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll find in the transcript that in 1995 this gentleman at least claimed that way. In 1995, this command post was fully operational when the western municipalities of Republika Srpska were under attack and the complete command post was moved in 1995 to this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I agree and I'll rephrase my description of his evidence if it suits Mr. Lukic that he said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: -- in 1992 it was not operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But then we should know -- I'm sorry. Can I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you have brought to the attention of Mr. Traldi something he could include in his question. He has offered to rephrase it. If there's any other matter you would like to bring to his attention which might cause him to even further rephrase the question, you have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Because in this transcript do we see about which period this gentleman is talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is clearly the point you are making. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before do you so, Mr. Traldi. I just wanted to say to Mr. Lukic, in any case, whatever you have told us is no basis for an objection. If you just make a note of that. It's different evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do agree with my colleague, Mr. Lukic. This is not an objection but this is a gentle -- gently presented information to Mr. Traldi so as to assist him in avoiding any errors. Mr. Traldi, that is how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I understood it the same way and appreciated it. Regarding the time-frame referred to in this portion of Colonel Vukelic's interview --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that no confusion should arise. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes. And just to make clear why our position is it's clear they're talking about 1992. It's in the context of discussions of visits by General Talic to the detention camp there. It's in the context of the discussion of the Mazowiecki visit which is in August 1992. That's mentioned at the top of the page. And it's in the context of the discussion of visiting Popovic, the commander during 1992 of the camp, that we see lower down on the page. That's the basis for my putting that this refers to 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and then now you'll rephrase the question as you offered, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, could the witness put his earphones on again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir -- sir, the question that I'll put to you is, you'd testified that the Manjaca forward command post, the Manjaca command post of the 1st Krajina Corps was not operational in 1992. The truth is, as Colonel Vukelic stated here, that it was working, that General Talic visited it, and also visited Manjaca camp; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, in order to provide a full answer, I cannot answer it by a simple yes or no. In the area of responsibility of the corps, there were eight command posts. All of them could be used, if needed, in order to successfully control the units. This included the command post at Manjaca. We, from the army, call it this way: The basic command post, the forward command post, the fake command post, and so on and so forth. So I was trying to recollect. I think there were eight command posts in different areas. Wherever the commander is, these posts could make sure that communication means were at his disposal to communicate with the units. He can even use the command post of an operational unit in order to successfully manage his units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we're at what would be the time for the break. I'd say I have just a few minutes left, pending whether I have any questions about the notes that I'm hoping we'll receive during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if it's just a few minutes. You know, a few minutes before the break usually are shorter than a few minutes after a break, Mr. Traldi, so I'll keep to you that for after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I can say it's eight questions, though it may be necessary to follow up on some of them, so less than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Less than ten minutes. That's accepted. Witness, we'd like to see you back after the break. We'll take a break until 10 minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, let's check again whether the videolink is functioning well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, Your Honour, we can see and hear you clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The same is true for this side of the videolink. Mr. Traldi, I'm looking at the clock. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And before I start, just to thank the Registry for their assistance in transmitting that material so quickly. Can we have P151. And I'll be looking for page 2 in the English, 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, this is a 1st Krajina Corps report from the end of May 1992. In the context of Mr. Lukic's questions about Muslims and Croats serving in the VRS, I'd direct your attention to point 5b, and we see in the first line down that: "After the actions in Kozarac, Kljuc, and Sanski Most, some conscripts of Muslim nationality have asked to be released from their [sic] units. They express their dissatisfaction with the massive destruction of their towns." You were also aware, weren't you, that non-Serbs conscripted into the VRS were not comfortable remaining because of the destruction it was inflicting on their communities?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that in the units of the VRS there were both Muslim and Croat soldiers and officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, answer the question. You knew that the massive destruction that the VRS was inflicting on their communities was why some of them were uncomfortable remaining; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about destruction for the most part in Kozarac where there was combat. It is normal that in the course of such activities that covered two or three days, although I wasn't present, that there must have been some destruction to facilities and buildings in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were aware of massive destruction of Muslim and Croat villages, just like the rest of the corps command and the Main Staff once they received this report; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about the destruction of a certain part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you knew, too, that other Muslims and Croats were dismissed pursuant to orders by General Mladic and General Talic from the VRS; right? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not dismissed. They were simply sent to other commands. I would say it was done with a view to resolving their status. They were not kicked out of the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They were sent to Belgrade to -- sir, they were sent to Belgrade to resolve their status; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And yesterday Mr. Lukic asked you the following question: "As far as you know - and you spent the war there - was the plan to occupy territory or hold on to territory which was not considered Serbian?" And you answered: "No such plan existed. The plan was, as I said, to maintain the territory where the Serbs were in the majority." I have a few simple questions for you about this. Prijedor, Sanski Most, and Kotor Varos, which we've discussed, were all Serb-minority municipalities in 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were fewer Serbs than Muslims living there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And after the operations by the 1st Krajina Corps, they were all controlled by the Serbs and had overwhelmingly Serb populations; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were dominant because Muslims left many of those parts, and they went to where they felt safer and where they could be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You testified this morning that there was no pressure on those people who were exchanged. Those people whose towns had been massively destroyed, obviously they had no choice but to go somewhere else; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And regarding -- regarding your evidence, again, that there was no -- that the plan was to maintain the territory where the Serbs were in the majority, there's evidence in this trial that by the end of 1992, the VRS had control of 70 per cent or so of the territory of Bosnia. Is it your position that that was all Serb territory?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not assert that. I know the size held by the 1st Corps. I'm not aware of the situation in the rest of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes or no: It's your position that the 70 per cent of the territory of Bosnia the VRS controlled at the end of 1992 was Serb territory?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was Serbian because it was still highly debatable whether others should be involved in determining whose territory it was supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, that completes my questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one follow-up question for the witness. But first Judge Moloto has one. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, at page 46, you were asked about the dismissal of non-Serb soldiers from the VRS by Mr. Talic and Mr. Mladic, and you said they were sent to other commands. Mr. Traldi said to you: "They were sent to Belgrade -- sir, they were sent to Belgrade to resolve their status; right?" You said: "Yes." I just want to follow up on that one. Their status in Belgrade was being resolved within the VJ, isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was resolved in Belgrade the way it was decided because there were centres in charge of personnel that kept the officers of the VRS on their registers. So in other words, their status was supposed to be resolved in Yugoslavia, in order to determine whether some of them have met the necessary conditions to be retired or that something else be done with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You haven't answered my question. They were resolved in -- because you said there were personnel centres, and it was personnel centre number 30 into which they were located which was a VJ unit, isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a command, rather than a unit, which dealt with the issue of status --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you saying -- let me ask you a question. Are you saying the 30th Personnel Centre was a unit of the VRS? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. What do you mean part of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi suggested to you that these soldiers were dismissed from the VRS. You said: No, they were not dismissed. They were sent to other commands. I'm saying to you, that command that you're saying they were sent to in Belgrade is the 30th Personnel Centre and I'm suggesting to that that is a VJ unit, not a VRS unit. So if they're there, it means they have left the VRS. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
