utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one question for you. You were asked about maintaining areas which were populated by a Serb majority. Then Mr. Traldi asked you about a few municipalities where you said that there was a Serb minority. Let me just check which ones they were. I think it was Prijedor -- let me just find it.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sanski Most, Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think a third one was mentioned as well. Now, often in answers and in documents we find reference to "loyal non-Serbs." What is the basis for claiming loyalty from non-Serbs where power had been taken over in municipalities in which the Serbs were in a minority, why would the majority be loyal and what's the basis for such a loyalty claim, if power was taken over by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Determining whether someone was loyal was the basis for those citizens, i.e., civilians, to decide whether they were willing to implement the laws and policies of the authorities then in power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, I do understand what loyalty means. But on what was the claim that they should be loyal where power had been taken over by a minority in those municipalities, on what was that claim based? Or just on having taken over power forcefully?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally think it was their choice to stay freely because they believed that they will continue being safe in their homes, with the neighbours with whom they used to be on good terms previously, rather than to change their place of residence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I established that you didn't answer my question. I gave it two tries. I have no further questions for you. Then we -- have the questions by the Bench triggered any need for further questions? If not, Mr. Kelecevic -- Yes, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sorry. If there's no objection to it, I've gotten part of the translation of the notes that have been sent to me that the witness took and I would have one question based on those. If that's agreeable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you shared the notes with the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see Mr. Lukic is nodding yes. Please -- one more question by Mr. Traldi, Mr. Kelecevic. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Traldi: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sir, under a reference to the document coming from Mr. Drljaca, what I understand to be a reference to that document that Mr. Lukic showed you, I'm told you have written, among other things: "Admission centre, they did not have accommodation and food." Which was the centre about which you -- which was the camp about which you wrote they did not have accommodation and food?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO KELECEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noted down what you read out to me. For the most part it had to do with Trnopolje and that there was a need to have them moved. I wrote down Drljaca's name because I found it difficult to remember that name and I know that he had a very important role when it involved the decision-making process by civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the person -- the extent of the information I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That was the only question I had, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Traldi, the proper question would have been in what context he wrote that down. Because it came immediately to my mind, having heard your questions, that it may well be, which is quite normal for a witness, to jot down some words which remind him of what the question exactly was and I think that should have been more transparent in your question. Mr. Kelecevic, this concludes your evidence. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to the videolink location and to testify, and I wish you a safe return home again. You are excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much. Good-bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we can close down the videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I am. A couple of remaining housekeeping matters from the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In one document there was a discussion of whether a village named was Baltina or Bastina. We've checked P7106, which is the excerpt from the census for Kotor Varos municipality, there is a Bastina listed and not a Baltina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at least it's clear now, which was not clear from the document yet, that it is a location.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Lukic, if you have any better location --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Regarding P7477 MFI, that's the letter from Bishop Komarica. The book from which it is taken is described in its text by the editor as containing "a selection of documents from the Bishop of Banja Luka, Monsignor Dr. Franjo Komarica and the Bishopric in Banja Luka written during the war from 1991 to 1995. There are many pastoral letters, appeals, interventions, reports, and denials," and P7477 MFI is part of a long collection of such that is included in that book. Third housekeeping matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, first, if it is MFI'd, we have -- the reason was that we asked for further information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, any objection against P7477?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We just now heard that it's a longer selection from this book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did understand that the selection is more than just this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Let me rephrase slightly for precision. The book includes a long collection of such correspondence. P7477 MFI is only the one that I showed the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We do not object to the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7477 is admitted into evidence. Third issue, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We're willing to agree that Spiro Nikovic has only one N. And fourth and finally, as a housekeeping matter, if I can just be excused, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are excused, Mr. Traldi. Is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would be Mr. Salipur?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The notes the previous witness wrote are now in the custody of the -- of the Registry although copies have been provided to the parties. Should they be kept or could they be ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't see any probational value. I don't know, the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- maybe does not share my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger. They have been destroyed once. Would we destroy them again?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would think not. Once we are in possession of those it's -- I mean, it's difficult, I agree, to imagine how they may be used in future. But as a matter of procedure, having received them, they were referred to in the examination to a minor extent, it seems more prudent to hang on to them. But, again, from a practical point of view, I don't think it is going to have much impact one way or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we're talking about the original, Mr. Lukic, Mr. Tieger, you've both received copies. If you could agree on that these copies are original copies and where the original -- it's pretty clear that we see even on the video that the witness is tearing them apart. So I have great difficulties in imagining that would ever be any dispute about the authenticity of your copies being a truthful copy of the original. And I think, under those circumstances, the -- there's no need to keep them for the Registry. So they can be torn apart again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may, before the witness sits down --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic waived his right to be here during procedural matters, and we will provide Your Honours with the written statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And Mr. Mladic is now present where you pronounced those words so -- the witness can be escorted in the courtroom. Mr. ... we'll then receive later the written confirmation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Salipur. Would you please stand. Mr. Salipur, before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Salipur, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You find Mr. Stojanovic to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Salipur.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Good day to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As is customary, I would like to ask you to slowly give us your name and surname.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: My name is Zdravko Salipur.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Salipur, at one point in time, did you give Mr. Karadzic's Defence a statement in writing, and did you answer the questions that were put to you then?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please see 65 ter 1D04065 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Salipur, at one point in time, you will see before you on that screen a document.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please take a look at the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Salipur, what you saw on this first and last page, is that the document that I asked you about a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's the document. And this is my very own signature in my own hand, and I wrote the date too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would just like to ask you a few things. Would you please take a look at the first page of this document. Let us focus on paragraph 1. Mr. Salipur, before appearing in this courtroom, during the proofing did you indicate to me that, in the meantime, your work status has been changed and that in line 4 in B/C/S, and in lines 4 and 5 in the English statement, it says that you are currently employed in the Rad public utilities enterprise in East Novo Sarajevo. You informed me that in the meantime you are retired and that this means that the correct information today is that you are a pensioner.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Yes. From the 1st of January, 2014, I officially ended my career and retired. Everything else is the same, including my address.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please a look at paragraph 31 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 31 of your statement, the penultimate line in B/C/S and the third line from the bottom in the English version. You told me that there was a typo there. The man whose name you mentioned is not Ljubo Obradovic. Rather, his name is Budo Obradovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I don't know how come this mistake happened. I knew the man personally. His name was Budo Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now that you've made these two technical corrections to your statement, if I were to put the same questions to you today, to the best of your knowledge and to the best of your recollection, now that you've taken the solemn declaration in this courtroom, would you fully stand by the statement that is before us?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Now, today, and in 100 years, if need be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender Mr. Zdravko Salipur's statement into evidence, 65 ter 1D04065.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Prosecution, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit Number D1112. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Also, I would like to tender four documents mentioned in this statement. According to 65 ter, they are marked 03605, 03651, 18486, and 03290.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, 65 ter 03605 receives number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives number 1113.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. And that's a D number. 65 ter 03651?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit Number D1114.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. 65 ter 18486?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit Number D1115.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. 65 ter 03290?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Has already been admitted as Exhibit Number P6524, admitted on 22nd May 2014. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, no need to further decide upon it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, with your leave, I would like to read out the summary of Witness Zdravko Salipur's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you intend to read a short summary. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness Zdravko Salipur is a pre-war inhabitant of Sarajevo and he will testify about the situation in Sarajevo prior to the breakout of the war, about the circumstances and conditions in the city before the elections of 1990, about the founding of the SDS and about his political involvement with the SDS Municipal Board in the municipality of Novo Sarajevo. He will also speak about the internal organisation of SDS in Novo Sarajevo and the establishment and tasks of the Crisis Staff, and also about the reasons behind the establishing of the Serb Municipal Assemblies in the territory of the city of Sarajevo and about the work of the War Presidency in that area. He will explain these documents concerning the structure and -- organisation and documentation of Crisis Staffs in the area of Novo Sarajevo and SDS organisations. Also the witness will testify about the arming of Muslims and Croats in the territory of the municipality of Novo Sarajevo and the existence of Crisis Staffs and paramilitary units established by the Muslim and Croat leaderships. This witness shall speak about what happened in a part of Sarajevo called Pofalici. Up until he was wounded and when the clashes took place in this area in May 1992 and upon his return from medical treatment in October 1992, he will speak about his experience and the attitude taken towards the civilian population, because he worked on humanitarian affairs through the Red Cross and in the area of Grbavica. Finally, he will speak about the shelling and sniping against this area that came from the territory that was under BH army control and about the freedom of movement in this area during the war. He explains his position and the sources of his knowledge as to how the authorities functioned in the territory of Grbavica. This was a brief summary of his testimony. And with your leave, Your Honours, I would just like to put a few questions to the witness in order to clarify his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed as you suggest, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please take a look at paragraph 7 of the statement which is now D1112.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Salipur, in your statement here, you are commenting upon a document on the establishment of the Serb municipality of Novo Sarajevo and you are referring to Article 3 of this document that has now been admitted into evidence in this case and its number is D1114. I would just like to ask you to explain the following to the Trial Chamber. The Serb municipality of Novo Sarajevo founded in this way, did it function, did it carry out its duties on the ground until the conflict broke out in Sarajevo? Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: I remember that document full well, the one that's mentioned in my statement, and it's true that on this day this so-called assembly was held, but it was not translated into practice. It was just before the war, perhaps a week before the war. It can be seen that it was sort of for the future, if the worst possible situation would occur. On the 4th of April war broke out in Sarajevo, so during those seven days, one could feel what would happen, so this was done out of caution. I would like to say, as I go back to that day, that this gentleman, Dr. Milivoj Prijic, it's mentioned here that he was elected as president of the municipality, and Mr. Branko Radan was elected president of the Executive Committee. It wasn't on that day that they were elected, at that assembly. Only a decision was made --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I think Mr. Stojanovic only asked you whether it carried out its duties and I think you've answered that question in the first line or the second line or the third of your answer. Please focus specifically on what is asked. If we want to know anything more, the parties will ask or we will ask. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the sake of the record, Mr. Stojanovic, you referred to an article which is mentioned in paragraph 8 of the statement. With a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: With document number from the Karadzic case. This is not 1D1114, what you said, it's not correctly recorded. It's the number P6524 which was already admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please always use the numbers assigned to the documents, both 65 ter and the exhibit number assigned to it, rather than to refer to the Karadzic numbering.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. So it will be that way, Your Honours. Maybe I should say that I was referring to paragraph 7 of this witness's statement and indicating paragraph 7 of this witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you referred to the wrong number. You referred to the Karadzic number rather than to the number assigned in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But in that case, you are right, Mr. Stojanovic, this is D1114.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Yes, I think I did the right thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Salipur, let us look at paragraph 11 of your statement, D1112. Please be as direct as possible and let us observe the time. This is what you say in paragraph 11 -- can you see that? "I had information about the military organisation and arming of Muslims and Croats in the area of the municipality ..." This is my question: In view of court practice here, tell us, as directly as possible, where does this information of yours come from about the military organisation and arming of the Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: When speaking about information, I had many information from friends and neighbours who saw this directly. I personally saw a lot as well. For example, night guards, large groups, armed. They would come during the night and leave in the morning. So I saw some of this personally and some things I found out about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who did you find this out from?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Neighbours from Pofalici, my area, towards the hill of Hum. Already in the month of February, the Patriotic League and the Green Berets dug trenches, they were armed, and the Serb population could not even get close. And they saw that members of the Ministry of Interior - that is to say, the police - brought weapons there during the night. They saw this themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I would like to ask for paragraph 24 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, I shall repeat once again now, its number is D1112. In English, can we move to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Here you discuss the events in the area of Pofalici. For the sake of precision, please tell us when this attack on your settlement occurred, that is to say, on Pofalici where you resided?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: It occurred on the 16th of May, early in the morning, from the direction I mentioned, which is Hum hill, where those armed formations had been observed. The attack lasted throughout the day and some 60, mostly civilians, people were killed in my settlement, including around 15 women and some people older than 90, as well as many elderly people between 70 and 80. There were many more wounded, over 200. I was wounded myself by a shell, and I was treated for five and a half months and then I needed crutches for another year. Let me just add, to this day, many people who were killed that day were never found. Their bodies, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you receive information about the number of those who were killed and wounded, as well as missing, the information you presented here in the courtroom today?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: That day, when I was wounded, I was taken away, and I did not have any idea how many people were killed and wounded in my settlement. After the end of my treatment, I was interested in finding out where my friends, relatives, and neighbours were so I investigated and looked for the bodies. With the assistance of the commission for tracing missing persons, I went to some locations where indications existed that they had been buried. However, we did not find many of them but we did come across traces indicating that they were dug up and moved elsewhere, according to the information in the possession of the commission. The location involved was a family graveyard in my settlement, and since I hail from that area, I know who was buried there and when, as well as in which part of the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the attack in the area of Pofalici, did the Serbian civilian population remain?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Very few remained compared to the overall number of the people who used to live there. Perhaps under 1 per cent. And over the period that followed, all trace was lost of them too. Nobody knows if they were killed or when they were killed, whether a week or a month later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that you lived there, what was the reason and motivation behind the attack on the area of Pofalici?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Before the witness answers, I would object to that question, as there's no foundation for how the witness could know what the motivation of the attack was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you lay a foundation, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Salipur, at the time or after you returned from treatment, did you gain any specific knowledge about the possible motivation and reason for the attack of the Muslim forces on that part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: I understood your question fully, and I do know what the motivation was. I can provide an answer. In Sarajevo, this settlement is across the town from Vrace and Grbavica. It is the only settlement on that side of the city where Serbs were in the majority. The Serb police and TO were established there in order to provide protection. Someone did not like that in geographical terms. Among the 350 Serbian houses in the settlements, there were perhaps 50 Muslim or -- and five or six Croatian households. For the month and a half between the 4th of April and the 16th of May, they moved about freely, going into town, to work and come back. Nobody touched them. The only thing that there was were the check-points aimed at preventing the entry of the Patriotic League members and the Green Berets, as well as the armed forces of BiH which were created later. Someone did not like the fact that geographically we were present there. There were reports in the media, on TV and the radio, that it was the goal of us living in Pofalici, the handful of us against the entire city of 600.000, to link up with the Marsal Tito barracks and then on further afield to Vrace. It was absolutely impossible to do, but someone obviously didn't like us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I appreciate that you asked for a foundation. Whether the witness gave it is a different matter. And I have another question. The witness referred to his medical treatment. Witness, are you referring to paragraph 29 of your statement which starts with: "After receiving medical treatment ..."? Is that what you referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was discussing the motivation for the attack when I was in Pofalici and when I was wounded. On the day of my wounding --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may be of assistance. I believe there is a reference to the witness being wounded on May 16th in an attack in the first paragraph of his statement, at the bottom of the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I wondered because paragraph 29 follows immediately a few redacted paragraphs of which, of course, we do not know what's in there. Mr. Stojanovic, could you assist us. Is there any reference there to the attack there? In the earlier -- in the paragraphs immediately preceding paragraph 29, where the witness refers to medical treatment, or is that -- is there nothing --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It is referred to, and there's some further detail about the fighting in the redacted portions in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the -- the only thing we know about the attack at this moment is what we find in paragraph 1? And all the details are redacted?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's also one part which discusses the situation preceding the fighting which is in paragraph 24, and that is why I sought to lay my foundation for this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the details about the attack, we are not privy to those, are we?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that part is redacted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I be of assistance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, thank you. Of course, Mr. Stojanovic, if you ask further questions about that situation and of being wounded, then, of course, I wonder why we're not receiving the detailed information about the attack. But I'll -- just please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There will also be a witness to discuss this, and that is probably why it was also redacted in the Karadzic case. In any case, there will be a follow-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: For the time being, I'd like to ask another question. Let us look at paragraph 30 of your statement. In paragraph 30, you discuss freedom of movement in the area of Vrace and Grbavica, and non-stop shelling and sniping from tall buildings and other facilities controlled by the Muslim forces. Many inhabitants were killed in that way of different ethnicities. Please tell the Court, as directly as possible and as specifically as possible, to your personal knowledge, which buildings or facilities were used by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to shell and snipe the area of Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: First of all, during the war, that area was one hell to live in. Grbavica was basically surrounded from three sides by the separation line with the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina between the army and the VRS. As regards the shelling, it was difficult to know where it was done from because a shell may be sent from a kilometre or two away. As regards the shooting and sniping and hundreds of victims that were targeted in Grbavica, the separation line was the Miljacka river, the length of over some 2 kilometres. It was the only division between the two sides. On the Army of the BH side, there is a promenade across the river and a certain number of buildings along it where the people did not reside. They were -- there were mostly offices and that's where the snipers were. Most sniping took place from the roof of the Faculty of Mathematics and Natural Sciences, close to the Miljacka river, somewhere halfway along the separation line of 2 kilometres. On the eastern end, some 100 metres away, was also the building of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina which commanded the entire part of town because of its height, not only Grbavica. There was much sniping from there. There was also sniping from the south-west side, from the building of Loris, which is the first building next to the football club Zeljeznicar stadium. However, there was one thing that could be observed the best, and that was a position of the Army of BiH which was, so to say, behind the back of entire Grbavica. They had a bunker or two there. They had dug a tunnel to them and engaged from there. I saw several civilians, including women, being hit in front of the building where I used to live, and we know to the metre where one can move and what the range was. The sniping place was only about a hundred metres away from the building where I lived and we could hear that one the most. All of the other shots we could hear came from a distance and it was difficult to distinguish whether there was some regular shooting or sniping. There was daily shooting for four years.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us the name of the building you have just described, as well as the area where the two bunkers were.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: It was called Debelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In terms of altitude, is Debelo Brdo higher than the settlement of Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Yes, much higher. It is in the direction of Mount Trebevic, at the foot of it. However, it is close, as the crow flies, not only to the separation line along the Miljacka but to Grbavica as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salipur, for these clarifications. And at this moment, the Defence has no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take break in a minute. I have one very short question for you. The source of the sniping fire, is it that you heard where it came from, or did you ever see snipers in those facilities you described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have in mind the sniping shooters who were active in Grbavica or against Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The ones you described as -- in your previous answer. Did you see them or did you hear that the sound was coming from the facilities you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was impossible to see. If I tried to see, I would be killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, I'm not saying that you should have seen it. I'm just inquiring in what the source of your knowledge of those facilities is. And apparently if you didn't see it, you may have heard that the sniper fire came from those facilities. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I could hear them. If I hear a shot and a woman falls down, you can see where she could have been hit from. She could not have been hit through a building. There must be an open area, a window, to engage. So even a layperson could conclude, on the basis of where a victim was killed or wounded, where the sniper was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you combined what you heard and what you did see as a result of the fire, that made you conclude where it must have come from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And there's another thing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you've answered my question. We take a break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: After the break you'll be cross-examined by Mr. File. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The parties are urged to see whether they can manage to conclude cross-examination and re-examination in this session, which takes one hour. We'd then have another close to -- after a break, we would have another 30 minutes to deal with procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, or even we could consider to continue then, but -- we would then have a short pause in order to allow Mr. Mladic to leave the courtroom because he has decided that he would waive his right to be present. So perhaps we would continue without a further break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be convenient for us, Your Honours, because we also have a scheduled call on General Mladic. So as far as we are concerned, we can proceed immediately after the examination of this witness ends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Salipur, may I urge you to focus your answer on the question, that is, not to go beyond what you are asked. Just focus on that. Mr. File will now cross-examine you. Mr. File is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: We heard at temporary transcript page 55 today that the witness statement that you've submitted in this case was the identical witness statement that you gave as evidence when you testified in the Karadzic case here at the ICTY. When you testified in the Karadzic case on the 17th and 18th of December, 2012, you told the truth; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Yes, 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And do you still stand by that testimony today?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'm going to read a quotation from your statement and then a quotation from your Karadzic live testimony and then I will ask you a question about it. So let's look at paragraph 8 of your statement, which is D1112. In that paragraph you say: "Crisis Staffs were formed in Serbian municipalities in accordance with the instructions of the government of the Serbian Republic of BH, and this was also done in the Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo." One sentence later you say that: "The Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo was formed in accordance with an excerpt from the above instructions." Those instructions are one of your associated exhibits, D1115, and they are dated on page 2 of that document as 26 April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now could I please have 65 ter number 32830, please. And if we could go to e-court page 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: This is your testimony in the Karadzic case from the 18th of December, 2012, at transcript page 31640, and there, after having been shown several Crisis Staff documents dating all the way back to December 1991, you were asked: "You must accept, yes or no, that the SDS did establish the Crisis Staff in Novo Sarajevo municipality at least as early as December 1991? Yes or no." Your answer was: "Well, yes, but in the context that I've mentioned in my answers, all of my answers, have a look at one of the earlier documents where it says that we have a co-ordinator for contact with other Crisis Staffs."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should slow down when you read.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So my question for you is: Isn't it true that your statement is wrong as to the time when a Crisis Staff was first formed in Novo Sarajevo? This was pointed out to you on cross-examination in 2012 but yet you failed to make any corrections or modifications to your statement here to account for this.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Oh, I don't know. I don't have that document shown here, the one that you're referring to in order to jog my memory. As far as I can remember, everything is the way I said in my statement, and the documents that were shown to me then, I gave the right answers to all of that in the record. The only thing that is mentioned is that in the Crisis Staff there were two men who were in charge of negotiating with the staffs of the other political parties, which meant that what was sought was the best possible solution already in that situation, before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, let's keep matters short. Mr. File puts to you that in your statement you say that on the 26th of April the Crisis Staff was formed and that in your Karadzic testimony you said that it was formed as early as December 1991. That's what is put to you. Which of the two is accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, of course, the end of 1991. On the 5th of April there was already a war going on. I mean ... I mean, if we're talking about the 25th of April, 1992, the war was already under way and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you don't have to explain why. Just, you say, it's 1991, which is not what is found in your statement. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like that ask you some questions about the Novo Sarajevo Crisis Staff. Your Crisis Staff received instructions on activity from the SDS Main Board; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: First the Crisis Staff had to be established, and for it to be established, there were instructions that were received and the instructions came from the government. Actually, from this -- this Main Board of the SDS, the Serb Democratic Party, and then that went to the lower organs, the municipal organs, and the Municipal Board. On the basis of these instructions establish the Crisis Staff, because the organisation had several members ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: In your testimony in the Karadzic case, you were asked whether you personally participated in the implementation of instructions received from the SDS Main Board in December 1991. And your answer was: "Yes, I did participate," and then you went on to emphasise that you were an elected member of the municipal assembly. That was at T31628 in the Karadzic case. Do you stand by that testimony today?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Yes. In 1990, at the elections, I was elected an assemblyman, and I was on the list of the Serb Democratic Party. And I was one of the founders in the municipality of Novo Sarajevo, one of the founders of the Serb Democratic Party, the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: The Novo Sarajevo Crisis Staff co-ordinated closely with Serb armed forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Serb armed forces did not exist at the time. The Serbian Democratic Party established the so-called TO as the war drew closer. The system in pre-war Yugoslavia was such that in addition to the armed forces there was the Territorial Defence comprised of the people themselves. It is rather complicated to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Well, to be specific, it's true that members of the Crisis Staff included the local chief of police, the local head of the Territorial Defence, and the secretary of the Secretariat for National Defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. File, the witness earlier apparently had problems with the time-frame. Could you give a time-frame for your question so that there's no confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: In early 1992, isn't it true that members of the Crisis Staff included the local chief of police, the local head of the Territorial Defence, and the secretary of the Secretariat for National Defence?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Yes. And this is why, in half a minute --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, no one asked you why. Just whether they were. You've answered that question. Please proceed, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we see 65 ter number 03625 -- sorry, 03635, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: As this comes up, you will see that this is a document reporting a Novo Sarajevo SDS Crisis Staff meeting dated 25 December 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: This does not seem to be the correct document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you just say it one more time, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: This is correct, the one that is showing now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So this a document reporting a Novo Sarajevo Crisis Staff meeting from the 25th of December, 1991. You will see that you have a task assigned to you under number 3. And if you go further down the page, it says: Tasks. They include list of military conscripts, first, second, third call-up, men between 17 and 65. Item 7 at the bottom says: Responsible for TO Territorial Defence insignia, Dragan Vucetic. So my question for you is that in December 1991, the SDS Crisis Staff was already participating in military-related activities such as drawing up lists of conscripts and dealing with military uniforms; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Yes. But the system was such, the system of All People's Defence, was such that we all had uniforms at home, irrespective of whether we were Serb, Muslim, or anything else. The TO was one thing; the army another.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be assigned Exhibit Number P7486. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7486 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Salipur, isn't it also true that by January 1992, the Novo Sarajevo Crisis Staff was calling all battalion commanders in the area to attend Crisis Staff meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Yes. But this TO was officially divided by that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we see 65 ter number 03640, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You will see this is a 29 January 1992 meeting minutes from the Novo Sarajevo Crisis Staff. And I just would like for you to verify item 10, which I believe is on page 2 of the B/C/S. This confirms your testimony that all the battalion commanders are to be called to the Crisis Staff meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit Number P7487. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter number 03243, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You will see that this is a Crisis Staff order from Novo Sarajevo dated 22 April 1992. Now, in this order, you see the Serbian Novo Sarajevo Crisis Staff issuing a military mobilisation order to local citizens that is subject to the Law on Military obligation and Military Court if it's not followed. Now, I note that at the beginning of this document it says that this order was issued on the basis of order taken by the Council of National Security of Serbian People. So it's true that this order was not a spontaneous independent decision by the Novo Sarajevo Crisis Staff; right? It was pursuant to an order that had come from above just a few days earlier. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Yes. Because by the time the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had been proclaimed by the Serbian MPs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the war was, by that time, some 20 days under way. But the VRS had still not been formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we look at P3027, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you tendering the current --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to tender that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit Number P7488. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Salipur, you will see that this is a SRBiH Ministry of National Defence decision concerning the establishment of the Territorial Defence as an armed force of the Serbian Republic of BiH dated 16 April 1992. This was the decision that the order we just looked at was implementing; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: This does not ring a bell, but in my view, there is a link with the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: That's fine if you don't know specifically. I'm going to shift topics slightly. It's also true that from the time the SDS party was created until the conflict began, Slavo Aleksic was a member of the Novo Sarajevo SDS Municipal Board; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, in the Karadzic case, you were asked about Aleksic's command of the Serbian Chetnik detachment in Novo Sarajevo and your response was: "... the unit under the command of Slavo Aleksic in the war was a company that was part -- I'm not sure whether it was the 1st or 2nd Battalion. For a time it was the Sarajevo and later the Romanija Motorised Brigade." Then you went on to say: "Well, Chetnik detachment and so on and so forth, that has nothing to do with it. You can see under whose command he operated." That at transcript page 31646 from that testimony. Do you still stand by that testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: I know for sure that the unit he commanded was part of the VRS as a company. It was included into the other units. They called themselves some sort of Chetnik movement, but that's a different thing. In any case, they were definitely part of the VRS as a military formation. My answer back then had to do with Slavo Aleksic. It was suggested that he had come from elsewhere as a volunteer, but in my statement I prove that he lived and worked in Sarajevo throughout the time and was a member of the SDS as of its establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I wasn't asking about where he came from. I'm going to show you a brief video-clip and then ask you about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter number 31015c. And, Your Honours, the transcript for this video has been confirmed by CLSS, so I believe it can be played just once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It may be played.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Journalist: From the day the war began, you were part of the Sarajevo defence and spent all your time at the Jewish cemetery, defending that part of Serbian Sarajevo. "Slavo Aleksic: Yes, I came to the Jewish cemetery on 21 April 1992, after the Muslim forces had broken through to a part of our territory. That day, 21 April, we were descending and clearing Grbavica. I was at the Vrbanja bridge and the Vrace Police Command ordered me to move together with my men to the positions at the Jewish cemetery, where we repelled the Muslim attack and inflicted heavy losses on them. They took away five or six civilian hostages in retaliation. They were later exchanged and from then on, from 21 April onwards, I was stationed at the Jewish cemetery. In May, around St. George's Day, I moved to a small barracks named Bosut, under Debelo Brdo. The communications centre was there, in a tunnel inside a hill. We held these positions until the Dayton Agreements were concluded, and we controlled the Jewish cemetery and Vrbanja, all the way from Debelo Brdo to the Vrbanja bridge, Ozrenska Street and so on. In other words, the area of Serbian Grbavica."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. File, you should put on the record the time when the video started to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I will have that for you in a moment, Your Honour. The beginning point is 14 minutes, 32 seconds. And it ends at 16 minutes, 5 seconds of the original video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Sir, you would confirm, first of all, that this is Slavo Aleksic speaking in this video?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And having seen this clip --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: What's he got to do with my testimony? It isn't clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Having seen this clip, would you accept that in April 1992 Aleksic was taking orders from the Vrace police command?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: In all of my statements, I say that the war began on the 4th of April. I lived in Pofalici, in a different part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: That wasn't the question, sir. That --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: I had no contact with that part where Grbavica, Vrace, and the Jewish cemetery are until Pofalici fell on the 16th of May. I didn't know what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'll stop you there. The question was whether you accept --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that in April 1992 Aleksic was taking orders from the Vrace police command. Now, there are three options: Either do you not accept it, or you do accept it, or you just don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I mentioned why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That answers the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender that video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit Number P7489.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to switch gears for a moment and ask you about the Novo Sarajevo Assembly in 1991. I'm going to start by playing you part of a recorded telephone conversation and then I will ask you some questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: This is going to be 65 ter 20458, and the duration of the first part that we're going listen to is 1 minute, 22 seconds, starting from 0.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Radovan Karadzic: Hello. Hi. "Unknown female voice: Hello. "Radovan Karadzic: Is this Djurovic's cabinet? "Unknown female voice: Yes, yes, it is. "Radovan Karadzic: Is President Djurovic there? "Unknown female voice: Is this Dr. Karadzic? "Radovan Karadzic: Yes, it's me. "Unknown female voice: Just a moment, please. "Radovan Karadzic: Hello. "Zarko Djurovic: Hello, Doctor. "Radovan Karadzic: How are you? "Zarko Djurovic: Pretty much so. "Radovan Karadzic: I called you yesterday but you were on the way between your home and work. "Zarko Djurovic: Yes. As soon as I arrived home I called, but you went to some kind of meeting. "Radovan Karadzic: Yes, I had another urgent thing. I wanted to say ... this thing with Neskovic, is it still on or not? "Zarko Djurovic: It is. "Radovan Karadzic: Could that wait a while so we can figure something out? "Zarko Djurovic: It can. It can wait a while so ... "Radovan Karadzic: All right. Then its settled. "Zarko Djurovic: Now, we have some discussions to attend today, there are some inter-party discussions. This guy Sarovic and engineer Soljic, they will hold talks today, so they'll probably leave it. I don't think they'll appoint anyone yet. "Radovan Karadzic: Take -- take that upon yourself, but don't -- let's see what we shall do, are we in his favour or what because -- "Zarko Djurovic: Uh-huh. "Radovan Karadzic: -- I have some more information here, I'll have it checked in about two or three days and then I'll ... "Zarko Djurovic: All right. "Radovan Karadzic: I'll see. By the way, how's business? "Zarko Djurovic: Well, it's pretty good. Nobody's nervous, I just gathered some people here, my closest associates and so. I can see here that this is being tapped and so on. Although, these people, they -- these guys from SDA, they are persistent and so ... "Radovan Karadzic: What do they want? "Zarko Djurovic: I see they are talking and they are constantly dissatisfied, following these people and so on. "Radovan Karadzic: Uh-huh. "Zarko Djurovic: Incidents all the time, constant discontent and so on. "Radovan Karadzic: We'll teach them the law pretty soon, because in Novo Sarajevo they blocked the work of the assembly."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Salipur, first of all, you recognise this as a conversation between Radovan Karadzic and Zarko Djurovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: I recognise both voices. 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We stopped at 1:21.4. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Zarko Djurovic was the chairman of the Executive Committee in Novo Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And hearing Karadzic's allegation that they - presumably this is the SDA - blocked the work of the assembly in Novo Sarajevo, would you agree that this conversation is taking place in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: I don't know when this conversation took place. I do recognise the voices. Zarko Djurovic was president of the Executive Council, coming from the ranks of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: That was the division of power after the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If you don't know, it's okay. Now I'm going to play what comes next in this telephone conversation which will be from 1 minute, 21.4 to the end, which is 2 minutes and 19 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Zarko Djurovic: Yes, they did. "Radovan Karadzic: I don't know to what extent that guy Setlivar is involved, but in any case the fact remains that they've blocked it. "Zarko Djurovic: Yes, they did. "Radovan Karadzic: And that we'll probably carry out some kind of reorganisation of the city as such. "Zarko Djurovic: Exactly. "Radovan Karadzic: And they can go to fucking hell. "Zarko Djurovic: Well, so they should. "Radovan Karadzic: And exactly where in Novo Sarajevo are their settlements? "Zarko Djurovic: Well, mostly it is Velesici, that can be joined to the centre without problems. "Radovan Karadzic: Yes, yes. How many of them are there in that area? "Djurovic: Well, about 6.000. "Karadzic: About 6.000. And what is the total number of them in the municipality? "Djurovic: In the municipality, there are ... you can't know for sure, but there are about 30.000 and then some. However, it seems they tampered with the census, but nothing can be done, otherwise that would ... "Karadzic: Census, huh? "Djurovic: Yes. "Karadzic: Yes, yes. "Djurovic: But there are about 30.000 for sure, and then there is Sanac, illegal settlement ... "Karadzic: Yes, yes. That, that can't be annexed to anything, right? "Djurovic: That can't -- well, it could, Sanac couldn't. "Karadzic: It can't, huh? "Djurovic: No, but that would be like a reservation, which we ... in all possible ways. Sanac is not that important anyway."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Salipur, I note that in your statement you say at paragraph 19: "I do not have, nor did I have, information to the effect that the Serbian leadership headed by Dr. Radovan Karadzic, by means of regionalisation, secretly grouped territories in BH which they considered to be Serbian so that these territories could secede from BH by force and possibly join Serbia and the Republic of Serbian Krajina, nor was this discussed in Serbian circles." Now, hearing this discussion between Radovan Karadzic and Zarko Djurovic, you would accept that this type of regionalisation was being discussed in Serbian circles; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: I don't know about these conversations in that sense. But following this recording and the text here, it just makes me laugh, really. Neither Karadzic nor Djurovic, they don't know the structure or anything of these settlements that they're talking about. It's like children were agreeing about things. I'm just telling you my opinion. I know Sarajevo, I was born in Sarajevo. And this Djurovic came later. I mean, he is a Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender that intercept, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. File, Mr. Registrar draws my attention to the fact that what was given on a CD is there indicated as being 65 ter 20458a. That's not exactly the same number as you used, I think. And that the total duration is 2 minutes, 18 seconds, which might also -- does that cover all of what we heard?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I accept those corrections, that's correct, it should be 20458a.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the time what we listened to, the intercept, was that all together -- was that all together 2 minutes, 18 seconds?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes, the entire intercept is 2 minutes and 18 seconds. We listened to it in two parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The two together then, we'll verify that. Mr. Registrar, could assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit Number P7490. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we please look at 65 ter number 10694.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There is one second missing, by the way. It says 2:18, whereas you indicated it was 2:19, but let's just accept that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You will see that these are the minutes of the 10th joint session of the Sarajevo SDS city and Executive Boards from the 27th of November, 1991, presided over by Jovo Jovanovic, chairman of the city board, Sarajevo SDS. There are three items in this document I would like to draw your attention to. On page 1 in both versions, agenda item 4, is titled: Regionalisation. If we could go to English page 4 and B/C/S page 5, you will see regarding item 4, in the middle of the page, that a detailed report was presented "about the results of the commission for carrying out regionalisation." And you'll see that that report was unanimously adopted. And now if we could go to English page 5 and B/C/S page 6, at the top of those pages, here this is Jovo Jovanovic who is recorded as stating, and I quote: "Very soon regionalisation would be carried out, and in areas with a Serbian majority and places where Serbs were owners of real estate, Serbian organs of government would be formed." Now looking at this document, it's true, isn't it, that a plan was in place and already being discussed in the SDS in Sarajevo at least by November 1991 to carry out a regionalisation that would create Serb territories. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this. I wasn't a member of any higher party echelons for the city of Sarajevo. All I know is the situation in the Serbian Democratic Party in the municipality of Sarajevo. I knew Mr. Jovanovic and I know about the meeting. I know that it was held in our municipal building. However, I didn't attend the meeting and I'm not familiar with any of these activities. This is something that never reached our Municipal Board, so this is something that I am only seeing now in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit Number P7491. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we please have P353. English and B/C/S pages 93 in both.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Sir, this is a notebook kept by Ratko Mladic and we're going to look at an entry from the 6th of June, 1992, at the Hotel Bistrica Jahorina entitled: Consultations on the military and political situation in SRBH.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we please go to English and B/C/S page 102.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Sir, here you see a reference to Neskovic. Now this is reference to the president of the Crisis Staff of Novo Sarajevo at that time in June 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. File, are you sure that these pages correspond? I have some doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: It may be that we need to go two more pages in the B/C/S. One more page, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we're on the right page, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now just to clarify, sir -- oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We were at the right page. I think we're not any --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes, I believe we were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One page back. No, perhaps one more --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: One more back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're now on the right page, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now I believe you can see a reference to Neskovic. He was the president of the Crisis Staff of Novo Sarajevo at that time, in June 1992; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: He was a government commissioner for the -- for Novo Sarajevo. That's what the title was. He was practically above the Crisis Staff and all of that. That post -- once the Crisis Staffs were established, the then-government introduced that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we go to English page 104 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what we looked at until now was page 102 in the English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes. And 103 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Indeed, 103, e-court page B/C/S. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: It may be that we need page 105 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So at the top of the page, you see "Karadzic," who says: "We could have gone for a compact and dispersed partition of Sarajevo if there had been the political means. Not all our wishes can be fulfilled, we have to be a mature people." Now that's the truth of the matter, that the Bosnian Serb leadership desired a partition of the city of Sarajevo if that had been possible; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the date is of the notes and the meeting, when this took place. In any case --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: For your information, it's the 6th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: In any case, Sarajevo was a divided city. It was never encircled. Throughout the war, it was a divided city. That would be the most correct way to describe it. It was divided at the beginning of the war. The war divided it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. Radovan Karadzic also participated significantly in local SDS affairs. For example, by personally attending at least ten different sessions of the SDS Municipal Board just in Novo Sarajevo alone, from the time of the 1990 elections until conflict broke out in 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Out of the six city assemblies, it was the municipality that had the strongest SDS presence. That is where the SDS won the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to shift to another topic. In your statement you talk about the Muslims arming themselves, in paragraph 11. And then in paragraph 24, you talk about Serbs having some weapons, like hunting rifles and pistols, that were legally in their possession. But isn't it true that the Novo Sarajevo SDS Municipal Board decided to give material support to Serbs who had been convicted of illegal arms trafficking in February 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: I am not aware of that kind of support. I do know about a situation with a convoy of weapons that was transported through our municipality's territory and that this was seized by the military police. I cannot remember it all precisely. This something that I heard. It was something that was happening far away from me, and I didn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'm going to try to refresh your memory. If we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. File --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- before you do so. I think the Chamber urged the parties to see whether they could conclude the examination-in-chief and cross-examination within this hour. Now we have seven minutes left. First, Mr. Stojanovic, as matters stand now, how much time would you need for re-examination? And I may point at the fact that you used 38 minutes in the examination of the witness rather than the 30 you assessed. How much time, as matters stand now, would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't need a lot. I just have a couple of questions so I am not going to take long at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that five minutes or is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think that would be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. File, I would like to urge you to conclude as quickly as you can now. And that means within the next five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may, with your leave, take approximately ten minutes to get through the -- if that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're running out of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to deal with procedural matters, so ten minutes is not okay. We already go beyond our schedule for more than five minutes and it's really urgent. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Could we look at 65 ter 03217, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, these are the minutes from the 13th Extraordinary Session of the SDS Novo Sarajevo Municipal Board dated 28 February 1992. You will see on item 5, you were present there. It says "Zdravko Malipur," but I would add that on page 5 of this document in both versions it quotes you as "Salipur" participating in this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we go to English page 6 and B/C/S page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So what you will see here is the issue arises regarding: "... problems of Serbs convicted for transport of arms in Vrace. They do not have money for paying the fine, trial expenses and lawyers' fees (200.000 dinars are needed)." And then it goes on to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: On the next page in the English, yes. And I believe it's next page in the B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: It says: "After discussion in which majority of members present at the meeting took part, the board reached the following conclusions: "... payment of 200.000 dinars for helping the Serbs convicted of transport in arms -- for transport of arms in Vrace has been approved." So it was not the case, as you suggest in your statement, that Serb arms were limited to legal possession of weapons; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: There's just a little time so I cannot explain this precisely. It depends on the time when they did have, when they didn't have. It changes from day to day. The situation changed from day to day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you're not invited to explain the whole of the situation. What Mr. File puts to you is that apparently from this document you could read that Serbs were convicted for transport of arms in Vrace and that money was needed for their defence, or further defence, and whether that does not indicate that Serbs were also dealing with illegal weapon business. If I understood your question well, Mr. File. Could you please answer that question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us whether, on the basis of this document, you agree that Serbs were involved in illegal arms as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally know who these people are. They broke the law and they had to pay the fine. Since they were our members, we approved a sum of money to help them out so that they don't have do go to prison. As for what weapons they were, who they were transporting them for, where they were supposed to be going, all these things I don't know anything about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: My last question relates to paragraphs 20 and 30 of your statement where you deny knowledge, in paragraph 20, that civilian authorities supported or were involved with the permanent removal of non-Serbs from territories claimed by Serbs; and in paragraph 30, where you say the non-Serbian population was allowed access to all public institutions, enjoyed all civil and human rights, and had freedom of movement in the whole of Republika Srpska. I'd like to show you Exhibit P307, please. When this comes up, you will see that it is an UN document from UNCIVPOL, an occurrence report from Sector Sarajevo regarding the expulsion of Muslim citizens from Grbavica Sector Sarajevo to the area of Novo Sarajevo dated 30th of September, 1992. It describes the area on page 1, that it is the Bristol Hotel area. The second paragraph says that the preliminary information confirmed that the expulsion was in progress. And then at the bottom paragraph on English page 1 and moving on to B/C/S page 2, it describes a scene that was totally out of control with the sound of shelling and gun-fire, people in a panic. The Red Cross confirmed approximately 300 Muslim civilians had been expelled. And then in English page 2 and B/C/S page 3, the penultimate paragraph, the report's author found it very strange that this specific area of the town was under shelling. And he said it appeared evident that the shelling was directed towards the Muslim civilians. Now I would also note that this was labelled by -- an expulsion by SRNA, the Serb media outlet, in P6527. And it also led to a protest from UNPROFOR Commander Morillon to Radovan Karadzic, which is P4592. Now this event appears to have taken place just a few days before you returned from Belgrade to Grbavica. It involved hundreds of people. It was serious enough to provoke a protest at the highest levels and it happened in precisely the part of Sarajevo that you returned to, but there's no mention of this in your description of the harmonious relations and life enjoyed by non-Serbs in Grbavica. So my question to you is: Why did you exclude this incident from your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Could you please show me this first page for a second again, please. As far as I can see, first of all, I'd never heard of this and it did not happen while I was at Grbavica. Secondly, as far as I can see, Hotel Bristol is mentioned in this document. Hotel Bristol is not in Grbavica. It was under the control of the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you say you never heard about it, which, I think, answers the question why you can't tell about it. Mr. File, you had used more than your five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And that's all I will use. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. File, before you sit down, do you have any intentions with respect to 65 ter 03217?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If I omitted to ask for that to be tendered, then I would ask for that now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You did omit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It shall be assigned Exhibit Number P7492. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Mr. Stojanovic, your five minutes start now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
