utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Salipur, at some point today in cross-examination you were asked if representatives of the police and commanders of police stations were members of Crisis Staffs and if you recall you tried to say that they were but you were stopped in your intention to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, Your Honours, it was page 75 of today's temporary transcript, lines 11 through 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you why were representatives of police stations represented on the Crisis Staffs at that time, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: I'll be brief. After the elections, when the authorities were set up, if the police commander was a Muslim, his deputy would be a Serb, or in case of the TO, the principle was the same. Each of those officials was a member to a Crisis Staff. As someone from a particular political party, they were given that position. That is what I wasn't allowed to explain. So on the same Crisis Staff there would be two people from different organisations: One from the SDS and another from somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Another question. At that time, according to the coalition agreements between the national parties participating in the division of power, were the staffs and duties also divided according to the ethnic key?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Yes. The chief of TO Staff was Idriz --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness kindly slow down and repeat the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you slow down and repeat the names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Salko Idriz, chief of the TO Staff in Novo Sarajevo municipality, pre-war chief, he assumed that position on behalf of the SDS and he participated in the attack on Pofalici when the 60 people were killed. His deputy was Momo Garic on our side, in our Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, I'd like to consult with the client briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Salipur, I'd like to thank you on behalf of General Mladic's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have no more questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No more questions from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Bench also has no further questions for you, Mr. Salipur, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you, questions put to you by the parties, and questions put to you by the Bench. I wish you a safe --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well. I would be happy if my testimony contributed to the reaching of the truth or anything of the sort. In any case, to assist you in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for the good wishes, and you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll just take a very, very short break in order to allow Mr. Mladic to leave the courtroom because he waived his right to remain present when we're dealing with procedural matters. We take a break of one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: --- Break taken at 2.56 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll deal with some procedural matters. We start with the first one. That's an oral decision on the admission of associated exhibits tendered through Witness Vladimir Lukic. The witness testified on the 8th through the 10th of September, 2014. From the original 88 tendered associated exhibits on the exhibit list submitted with the Defence's Rule 92 ter motion, 11 documents were admitted into evidence during Lukic's testimony. On the 25th of November, 2014, the Defence submitted a revised exhibit list via e-mail and withdrew 11 of the originally tendered associated exhibits. An additional six documents were admitted into evidence pursuant to the Chamber's decision of the 16th of February, 2015. With regard to document bearing 65 ter number 1D5295, the Chamber notes that it was admitted as part of Exhibit P2508 on the 22nd of June this year, and this can be found at transcript page 36159 through 60. Accordingly, the Chamber will now decide on the remaining 59 documents tendered as exhibits associated with Lukic's witness statement admitted as Exhibit D626. The Chamber recalls that documents can be an admitted as associated exhibits if they form an inseparable and indispensable part of the witness's written testimony. In order to satisfy this test, the tendering party must demonstrate that the witness's statement would be incomprehensible or of less probative value without admission into evidence of the associated exhibits. The Chamber has discussed its interpretation of the applicable law at transcript pages 530 to 531, and 5601 to 5603, and in its written decision of the 23rd of July and another one, the 7th of February, 2013. The Chamber finds that without some of the tendered documents, it would not be able to comprehend the witness's statement and for this reason finds that these documents form an inseparable and indispensable part of Lukic's written statement. The Chamber therefore admits the following 22 documents bearing Rule 65 ter numbers 1D2447 up to and including 1D2449, Exhibit 1D2465, Exhibits 1D2472 up to and including 1D2474, documents 1D2478 up to and including 1D2480, document 1D2484 -- documents, I should say, 1D2484 up to and including 1D2487, document 1D2489, 1D2490, 1D2496, 1D2500, 1D4403, 1D5284, 1D5289, and 21766 into evidence as associated exhibits to Exhibit D626. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to assign exhibit numbers to the documents admitted into evidence. With regard to the remaining 37 documents, the Chamber finds that they either restate the witness's written evidence or in some instances lack any relations with the document. Therefore, these documents do not form an inseparable and indispensable part of Exhibit D626, and the Chamber further finds that the exclusion of these documents does not result in a lesser probative value of Exhibit D626 and consequently denies their admission. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. The next decision I'll deliver is the decision on the Defence's responses to the Prosecution's notices regarding the disclosure of the expert reports of Svetlana Radovanovic, Dragic Gojkovic, and Mile Dosenovic. On the 9th of February, the 13th of February, and the 10th of April, 2015, the Defence filed notices of disclosure of three expert reports authored by Radovanovic, Gojkovic, and Dosenovic respectively, pursuant to Rules 94 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Prosecution filed its respective notices on 11th of March, 16th of March and 30th of April. On the 25th of March, the 30th of March, and the 12th of May, the Defence filed its responses to the Prosecution's notices. On the 1st of April, 7th of April, and the 19th of May, the Prosecution requested leave to reply and replied. On the 13th of May and on the 22nd of May, for the latter, the Chamber delivered its decisions on the expertise of these experts but deferred its decision on the 25th of March, 30th of the March, and 12 May filings. This can be found at transcript pages 35582 through 585, and 36073 through 74. On a preliminary note, the Chamber considers the Defence's response filings of the 25th of March and the 30th of March to be akin to a motion. As a result, the Prosecution had an opportunity to respond to these motions and, accordingly, the Prosecution's requests for leave to reply are moot. The Defence submits that the Prosecution's notices do not comply with the Chamber's previous guidance on Rule 94 bis filings insofar as they failed to provide any specificity in relation to the Prosecution's objections. In this regard, the Defence submits that the Prosecution should be subject to the same Rule 94 bis filing standard as the Defence. The Defence further submits that the Prosecution should be precluded from challenging the methodology and subject matter of the three reports and that its cross-examination of the expert witnesses should be limited to seeking explanation of the reports' conclusions. The Prosecution submits that the Defence misinterprets the Chamber's guidance. It also argues that the guidance does not apply to the current situation as the Prosecution's position in relation to the issues challenged by the three Defence expert witnesses is already on the record. The Prosecution further submits that the Defence's proposed remedy is not contemplated by the rules and should therefore be denied. With regard to the Defence's first argument, the Chamber considers that the Prosecution has indicated in its notices the parts of the three reports it intends to challenge. Recalling its guidance on 5th of December, 2011, and the 11th of January, 2012, the Chamber notes that the parties are advised to be as specific as possible by identifying which sections of the reports it wishes to challenge and provide reasons for any challenges. The Chamber notes that the aforementioned guidance was issued prior to the start of the case at the stage of the proceedings where there was uncertainty as to which aspects of the Prosecution's expert evidence would be challenged by the Defence. In the current stage of the proceedings and in light of the evidence presented by the Prosecution, the position of the Prosecution and the issues in dispute are better known to the parties. The Chamber further notes that some of the aforementioned Defence experts have indicated in what respect they take issue with the reports of the Prosecution experts. The degree of specificity envisaged by the guidance does not necessarily need to be made in a party's Rule 94 bis under (B) notice, but in order to expedite the proceedings and to ensure clarity, should be communicated to the tendering party well in advance of the expert's testimony. The Chamber considers that the Prosecution could have specified more clearly and in greater detail the parts of the reports that it intends to challenge. Concerning the Defence's second submission, the Chamber recalls that Rule 90(H) does not provide for such limitations. The Chamber also recalls its decisions on the expertise of Reynaud Theunens and Ewa Tabeau dated the 25th of September and the 7th of November, 2013, respectively, in which it considered that arguments relating to the content and methodology of expert reports can and should be addressed during cross-examination. This can be found at transcript pages 17437 through 440, and 18874 through 75. Based on the foregoing and pursuant to Rule 54 of the Rules, the Chamber denies the Defence's requests. However, the Chamber invites the Prosecution to further specify its objections to the expert reports of Svetlana Radovanovic, Dragic Gojkovic, and Mile Dosenovic, and considers that these objections can and should be addressed during cross-examination of the witnesses. This concludes the Chamber's decision on this matter. I move on. Oral decision on the expertise of Witnesses Mitar Kovac. The Chamber -- on the 17th of February, 2015, the Defence filed a notice of disclosure of Milos Kovac's report pursuant to Rule 94 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Prosecution filed its notice pursuant to the same rule on the 19th of March, submitting that, while it does not challenge the status of Kovac as a military expert or the relevance of his report, it does not accept the conclusions of his report, and, therefore, wishes to cross-examine him. On 2nd of April, the Defence filed a response to the Prosecution's 19th of March submission. On the 9th of April, the Prosecution sought leave to reply and filed a reply to the Defence response. Today, the Chamber has addressed similar party submissions corresponding to those of 2 and 9 April regarding other experts and takes the same position here. With respect to the applicable law concerning expert evidence, the Chamber recalls and refers to its 19th of October, 2012, decision concerning expert witness Richard Butler. On the basis of Kovac's curriculum vitae and considering that the Prosecution does not dispute Kovac's qualifications as military expert, the Chamber is satisfied that he has specialised knowledge and expertise, and that such knowledge and expertise may be of assistance to the Chamber in assessing the expert evidence presented by the Prosecution during its case in-chief. With regard to the Prosecution's request to cross-examine the witness, the Chamber notes that the Defence plans to call Kovac to give evidence. The Prosecution will therefore have the opportunity to cross-examine him. Based on the foregoing, the Chamber decides, pursuant to Rule 94 bis, that Kovac may be called to testify as an expert witness and that he shall be made available for cross-examination by the Prosecution. The Chamber defers its decision on admission of his expert report to the time of his testimony. The Chamber now directs the Defence's attention to a preliminary observation regarding Kovac's report. The Chamber observes there is information in the report that is beyond the scope of the witness's area of expertise. Apart from discussing matters related to the witness's military expertise, the report focuses quite heavily on ethnic, religious, demographic, and historical elements. For example, at pages 102 through 104 of his report, the witness appears to challenge the work of expert demographer Ewa Tabeau in general based on the writings of a demographer called Stevo Pasalic. Various sections of the report also contain tables and figures of unsourced demographic data. I refer to pages 22, 102, and 107. And three attachments to the report, which the Chamber observes are not in fact attached, intend to inform the Chamber on the ethnic composition of the population of Sarajevo and of Bosnia. The Chamber has not received material establishing the witness's expertise as a demographer, a historian, or a sociologist. As a result, it expects the parties to focus their examination of the witness on those aspects of the report that relate to his analysis of the military. The Chamber will decide upon completion of Mitar Kovac's testimony on the admission into evidence of his report or portions thereof as may be the case. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. I now move to a few remaining issues from the testimony of Svetozar Andric. On the 9th -- 29th of April, 2015, P7358 and P7360 were MFI'd, pending receipt of B/C/S translations. On the 19th and the 21st of May, 2015, the Prosecution informed the Chamber and the Defence by e-mail that the translations were uploaded into e-court under the doc ID numbers 0265-0037-BCST and R012-2224-BCST respectively. The Chamber has instructed to attach these translations -- the Registry. The Registry is instructed to attach these translations and the Chamber admits P7358 and P7360 into evidence. Also on the 29th of April, D1038 was MFI'd, pending receipt of an English translation. On the same day, the Defence informed the Prosecution and the Chamber that the translation was uploaded into e-court under doc ID number 1D19-2016. And on the 30th of April, the Prosecution stated that it had no objections. The Registry is instructed to attach the translations and the Chamber admits D1038 into evidence. Next item, two exhibits, P7347 and P7362, were reserved -- these numbers were reserved on the 28th and the 29th of April, 2015, pending the Prosecution selecting the excerpts of the two documents to be tendered. On the 4th of May, the Prosecution informed the Defence and the Chamber that it had selected the excerpts which are uploaded under 65 ter numbers 32499a and 2364a. The Defence has not objected to admission. The Chamber instructs the Registry to replace the current P7347 and P7362 with the mentioned 65 ter numbers and admits them into evidence. Next item is a reminder about Rule 92 bis motions. On 29th of June, the Defence stated that it would start filing its Rule 92 bis motions during week of 6th of July. To be found at transcript page 36439. As of now, no such motions have been filed. As Rule 92 bis motions require significant time and effort for the responding party, as well for the Chamber, this is not something that the Defence can postpone until the last minute. The Chamber urges the Defence to start filing its Rule 92 bis motions as soon as possible. Then I move to the next decision to be delivered. It's a decision on the admission of P7381. On the 12th of May, 2015, P7381, a proposal for the appointment of officers to the 1st Birac Infantry Brigade dated the 23rd of August, 1992, was marked for identification during the testimony of Dragan Todorovic. The Defence objected to its admission, stating that the witness had no knowledge about the document and that it lacked sufficient indicia of authenticity. This can be found at transcript page 35420. The Chamber granted the parties time to make additional submissions, if any, until the 15th of May. No submissions were received by the set deadline. A reminder e-mail sent by the Chamber's staff on the 20th of May also did not result in any further submissions by the parties. The Chamber will therefore now decide on the admission of P7381. The Chamber recalls that the applicable law for the admission of evidence is set out in Rule 89(C) of the Rules which allows a Chamber to admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value. With regard to the Defence's objection that the witness had no knowledge about the document, the Chamber recalls that this is not a requirement for tendering it through a witness, as long as the document's content is sufficiently linked to the content of the witness's testimony. On the issue of authenticity, the Chamber recalls that prima facie proof of reliability on the basis of sufficient indicia is enough at the admissibility stage. The Chamber has analysed P7381 in this light, a document which was allegedly generated on the 23rd of August, 1992, by the Birac Infantry Brigade. While the Chamber acknowledges that this is the same brigade the witness was a member of, the document, however, lacks other relevant indicia of reliability such as an addressee. Moreover, it does not bear a stamp or signature, which raises the additional question of whether the document is, in fact, complete. The witness himself was not able to provide information about the document that would have guided the Chamber. Finally is the relevance of the document unclear to this Chamber. For these reasons, the Chamber hereby denies the admission into evidence of P7381 without prejudice. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. I move to an oral decision on the admission of Exhibits P6858 and P6859. On the 29th of October, during the cross-examination of Witness Slavko Kralj, the Prosecution showed the witness a photograph, asked him to comment on it, and then tendered the photograph along with a related four-page transcript of Johannes Rutten's testimony from the Krstic case. These were later marked for identification as Exhibits P6858 and P6859 respectively. The Defence objected to the admission of the transcript excerpt, P6859, on the grounds that Rutten should be called to testify. The Chamber understood the Defence's objection to mean that the transcript of Rutten's previous testimony could not be offered in lieu of his testifying in the present case unless tendered pursuant to Rule 92 bis of the Rules. The Prosecution submitted that, pursuant to Rule 89(C), the Chamber has a great deal of discretion in the admission of evidence, and that Rule 92 bis should not be apply to such a short excerpt of testimony. This discussion can be found on transcript pages 27475 to 27478. Rule 89(C) of the Rules allows the Chamber to admit any relevant evidence it deems to have probative value, while Rule 92 bis is the lex specialis for out-of-court statements prepared for the purpose of legal proceedings and tendered in lieu of oral testimony before the Tribunal. The Chamber notes that the witness Kralj was unable to comment on P6858, the event depicted in the photograph, or provide any information about the relevant context, and for these reasons, the Chamber finds that P6858 is not relevant for purposes of admission. While the Chamber agrees with the Prosecution that it maintains a great deal of discretion with regard to the admission of evidence pursuant to Rule 89(C), it finds no support for the argument that the applicability of Rule 92 bis somehow depends on the length or the content of the proffered evidence. Considering that the excerpt of Rutten's Krstic testimony has been tendered in lieu of Rutten's oral testimony before the Tribunal, the Chamber finds that Rule 92 bis applies and not Rule 89(C) as argued by the Prosecution. And for these reasons the Chamber denies the admission into evidence of P6858 and P6859 without prejudice. And this concludes this decision. The next decision -- let me just think about it one moment. Next decision, a decision on the tendering of associated exhibits for Vojo Kupresanin. On the 10th of October, 2014, the Defence filed a Rule 92 ter motion for Kupresanin tendering 46 associated exhibits. On 11th of November, the Prosecution noted that seven of the 46 associated exhibits were already in evidence. On the 17th of December, the Prosecution filed its e-mail of the 8th of December to the Chamber and the Defence which set out its position regarding the remaining 39 associated exhibits; namely, that it objected to the admission of six of them. On 2nd of March, 2015, the Defence filed its response and clarified that two of the documents objected to were already in evidence and that three others had previously been withdrawn. The remaining associated exhibit objected to was admitted on the 14th of May, 2015. The Chamber also puts on the record that on the 20th of May, the Defence, via e-mail, withdrew two further documents. The Chamber notes that documents bearing 65 ter numbers 2628 and 06884 were admitted, P7004 and P7006 respectively. Accordingly, the Chamber will decide on the remaining 29 documents. The Chamber recalls that documents can be admitted as associated exhibits if they form an inseparable and indispensable part of the witness's written testimony. In order to satisfy this test, the tendering party must demonstrate that the witness's evidence would be incomprehensible or of less probative value without the admission of the relevant associated exhibits into evidence. The Chamber has discussed its interpretation of this case law at transcript pages 530 to 531, and 5601 to 5603, and in its written decisions of the 23rd of July, 2012, and 7th of February, 2013. The Chamber has reviewed the Kupresanin statement against the background of the test for admission of associated exhibits and finds that each of the following 19 documents forms an inseparable and indispensable part of the statement to the extent that the statement would be incomprehensible or of less probative value without them. D989 and documents -- and D989 is marked for identification, and further documents bearing Rule 65 ter numbers 3016, 7197, 16868, 17222, 1D2433, 20153, 16121, 6875, 20268, 20435, 1D2027, 20520, 17208, 2559, 2604, 16132, 16135, and 1D2867, and therefore admits them into evidence. The Registry is requested to assign numbers by way of filing an internal memorandum. The Chamber finds that ten remaining documents do not form a inseparable and indispensable part of Kupresanin's statement, as they to some extent restate the witness's written evidence or in some incidents are not sufficiently related to the content of the statement. The Chamber further finds that the exclusion of the remaining documents does not result in the statement having lesser probative value. Consequently, the Chamber denies their admission into evidence and this concludes the Chamber's decision. We have a little bit less than ten minutes remaining. And the Chamber also invites you to update us on whether you have made up your mind as far as the list of witnesses is concerned. We're still waiting for further information.
